findings.title: Documented API Interface
findings.description: No programmatic interface of any kind exists. The only integration surface is the VB6 form `frmCustomer` in `frmCustomer.frm`, which opens an ADODB connection directly to a Microsoft Access file (`Provider=Microsoft.Jet.OLEDB.4.0;Data Source=S:\CRM\sales.mdb`, lines 19-21) and executes inline SQL from a button click handler (`cmdSave_Click`, lines 24-34). README.md documents the integration model as 'a Microsoft Access (.mdb) file on a shared network drive' with a nightly DTS/SSIS sync to SQL Server — i.e. file-based and database-level exchange. Searched for: REST route definitions, Spring/Flask/Express handlers, `.graphql`/`.gql`, `openapi.*`/`swagger.*`, AsyncAPI, `.smithy`, RPA/Selenium scripts — zero results across the 3 tracked files.
findings.gap: There is no REST, GraphQL, gRPC or AsyncAPI interface. Any agent integration would require direct Jet/OLEDB access to an .mdb file on an SMB share, or UI automation of a Win32 form — both brittle, unauditable, and unsupported for concurrent machine-speed callers.
findings.recommendation: Expose customer operations behind a service API before any agent integration. Target: migrate the Access data to a managed relational store (Amazon RDS/Aurora) and front it with a documented HTTP API (API Gateway + application service) that becomes the single agent-facing contract; retire direct .mdb access.

findings.title: Idempotent Write Operations
findings.description: `cmdSave_Click` (frmCustomer.frm lines 24-34) performs an unconditional `INSERT INTO Customers (Name, CreatedBy, CreatedOn)` with no idempotency key, no business-key uniqueness check, and no read-before-write. Because errors are swallowed by `On Error Resume Next`, the caller cannot distinguish 'insert succeeded' from 'insert failed', and the user-facing message explicitly instructs 'Try again.' — a retry path that creates duplicate customer rows. No unique constraint is declared anywhere in the repository (no schema or migration files exist).
findings.gap: No idempotency mechanism: retries duplicate records. Combined with swallowed errors, the retry instruction is built into the UI.
findings.recommendation: Introduce an idempotency key (or a natural-key unique constraint on Customers) and make the write path return a deterministic result for repeated identical requests before exposing writes to any retrying caller.

findings.title: Machine Identity Authentication
findings.description: There is no authentication mechanism. The application connects to the data store with a single hardcoded Jet database password (`Private Const DB_PW As String = "crm2005pw"`, frmCustomer.frm line 8; used in the connection string at lines 19-21) shared by every copy of the EXE on every field laptop. Caller identity is taken from `Environ("USERNAME")` (line 27) — a client-side environment variable that is trivially spoofable and is not authenticated by the database. Searched for: OAuth2/client-credentials flows, API keys with principal attribution, mTLS config, service accounts, Cognito/IAM/API Gateway authorizers — none present.
findings.gap: No machine identity, no principal authentication, and no trustworthy principal attribution. Every caller is indistinguishable at the data layer, so no downstream authorization or audit decision can be relied upon.
findings.recommendation: Introduce an identity provider and machine-identity authentication (e.g. OAuth 2.0 client credentials or IAM-authenticated service access) in front of the migrated datastore, with per-agent principals and no shared database credential.

findings.title: Scoped Permissions (Least Privilege)
findings.description: Authorization is binary and shared: possession of the Jet database password (`DB_PW`, frmCustomer.frm line 8) grants full Jet/OLEDB access to `S:\CRM\sales.mdb` (line 7). There is no role model, no per-caller permission set, and no mechanism to grant read-only access to a subset of tables or rows. No IAM policies, resource policies, or condition keys exist (no IaC in the repository).
findings.gap: All authorization is coarse-grained — a single shared credential conveys full database access, so an agent identity cannot be scoped down to read-only or to specific resources.
findings.recommendation: Define scoped roles at the service/datastore layer (read-only, customer-write) and bind agent principals to the narrowest role once AUTH-Q1 identity exists.

findings.title: Action-Level Authorization
findings.description: No action-level authorization exists. `cmdSave_Click` (frmCustomer.frm lines 24-34) issues raw SQL over an ADODB connection opened with full database rights; the same credential can `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` any table in `sales.mdb`. Searched for `canRead`/`canWrite`/`canDelete`-style checks, ABAC/RBAC definitions, permission matrices and method-level authorization — none present.
findings.gap: The data layer cannot allow read without also allowing delete. An agent granted the ability to read customers inherently has the ability to destroy them.
findings.recommendation: Enforce action-level permissions in the service layer introduced in API-Q1 (separate read, create, update, delete grants per principal) and revoke direct SQL execution rights from callers.

findings.title: Identity Propagation and Delegation
findings.description: No identity propagation or delegation exists. The only identity signal is the client-side value of `Environ("USERNAME")` string-concatenated into the `CreatedBy` column (frmCustomer.frm line 27). There is no token, no JWT parsing, no on-behalf-of flow, and no way to distinguish a caller acting as itself from a caller acting on behalf of a specific user — the archetype is `stateful-crud`, so no INFO downgrade applies.
findings.gap: An agent acting on behalf of a user cannot be bounded by that user's permissions, and the `CreatedBy` attribution it writes is caller-asserted and unverifiable.
findings.recommendation: Carry a verified identity (token-based, with distinct agent-as-self and agent-on-behalf-of-user modes) through the service layer and populate `CreatedBy` from the authenticated principal, never from a client-supplied environment variable.

findings.title: Credential Management
findings.description: Database credentials are hardcoded in source and compiled into the distributed binary: `Private Const DB_PATH As String = "S:\CRM\sales.mdb"` and `Private Const DB_PW As String = "crm2005pw"` (frmCustomer.frm lines 7-8), interpolated into the connection string at lines 19-21. README.md independently records this as a known issue: 'ODBC connection string with credentials embedded in the EXE'. The password value indicates no rotation since 2005. No secrets manager, Vault client, or parameter-store reference exists; `.gitignore` excludes `.env` files but no secret-management mechanism replaces them.
findings.gap: A static, unrotated, shared credential is embedded in code and in every deployed EXE. Anything that can read the binary or the repository — including a prompt-injected agent with file access — obtains full database access.
findings.recommendation: Move the credential to a managed secret store (AWS Secrets Manager) with rotation, remove the constants from source, and rotate the existing password immediately since it is exposed in version control history.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: There is no audit log. The single write path (`cn.Execute sql`, frmCustomer.frm line 29) records only a `CreatedBy` column populated from the client-controlled `Environ("USERNAME")` value (line 27) inside the same mutable Access file it is auditing. Errors are discarded by `On Error Resume Next` (line 28), so failed writes leave no trace at all. Searched for CloudTrail/CloudWatch configuration, log retention policy, object-lock log storage and any logging framework — none present (no IaC, no config files beyond `.gitignore`).
findings.gap: No immutable, tamper-evident record of write operations and no verifiable principal attribution. Agent-initiated writes could not be reconstructed, attributed, or proven for compliance or forensics.
findings.recommendation: Emit an append-only audit record (authenticated principal, operation, timestamp, outcome) to tamper-evident storage outside the application's own writable datastore before enabling any write-capable agent.

findings.title: Agent Identity Suspension
findings.description: There is no revocable identity to suspend. Access is conveyed by the shared compiled-in password (`DB_PW`, frmCustomer.frm line 8); revoking it requires changing the Jet database password and recompiling and hand-redistributing the EXE to every laptop — README.md states 'Distribution: EXE copied to each laptop by hand' and 'No installer; deployment is "copy the EXE and the .mdb template"'. No API key revocation, role deactivation, or account-disable mechanism exists.
findings.gap: A misbehaving caller cannot be isolated without revoking access for every user of the application simultaneously.
findings.recommendation: Issue per-principal credentials through the identity provider from AUTH-Q1 so a single agent identity can be disabled immediately without affecting other callers.

findings.title: Compensation and Rollback
findings.description: No transaction, compensation, or rollback support exists. `cmdSave_Click` (frmCustomer.frm lines 24-34) executes a bare `cn.Execute sql` with no `BeginTrans`/`CommitTrans`/`RollbackTrans`, no saga or compensating action, and no undo path. `On Error Resume Next` (line 28) actively discards the failure signal, and `Form_Unload` closes the connection the same way (lines 36-40). README.md records that the Access file 'corrupts under concurrent writes (~monthly)' — partial-write damage is an observed operational reality, not a hypothetical.
findings.gap: A multi-step or failed write leaves the database in a partial state with no rollback and no recorded failure. There is no mechanism to undo an agent-initiated write.
findings.recommendation: Wrap write sequences in explicit transactions with error propagation (and provide an explicit reversal operation for each exposed write) before allowing any autonomous write caller.

findings.title: Concurrency Controls
findings.description: No concurrency control exists. The write is a fire-and-forget `cn.Execute` against a Jet/OLEDB file on an SMB share (frmCustomer.frm lines 19-21, 29) with no version field, no `If-Match`/ETag equivalent, no `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, and no conflict-resolution logic. The only concurrency handling is a `MsgBox` telling the user 'record may be locked... Try again.' (line 31). README.md confirms the consequences: 'Access .mdb on a file share corrupts under concurrent writes (~monthly)' and 'No real multi-user locking; "record locked" errors are common'.
findings.gap: Concurrent writers corrupt the data file — an already-observed monthly failure. Multiple concurrent agent instances would multiply write contention on a store with no locking discipline.
findings.recommendation: Migrate off file-share Jet to a server-based database with real transaction isolation, and add optimistic concurrency (row version) on customer records before allowing concurrent write callers.

findings.title: Circuit Breakers and Resilience
findings.description: The application depends on an external resource — the `S:\CRM\sales.mdb` file on an SMB share (frmCustomer.frm line 7, opened at lines 19-21) — with no resilience controls: no timeout on `cn.Open`, no retry or backoff, no circuit breaker, and no connection-failure handling (`Form_Load` has no error handler at all, lines 17-22). README.md notes the dependency is a single point of failure: 'File share is a single Windows file server with no failover'.
findings.gap: A slow or unavailable file share produces an unhandled failure or an indefinite hang, and repeated caller retries apply unbounded pressure to a dependency with no failover.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit connection timeouts and bounded retry with backoff around data access, and introduce a circuit breaker in the service layer from API-Q1 so dependency failure degrades predictably.

findings.title: Blast Radius and Transaction Limits
findings.description: No business-domain limits exist. `cmdSave_Click` (frmCustomer.frm lines 24-34) imposes no cap on records created, no bulk-operation size limit, no per-caller quota, and no spend threshold; nothing in the repository is configurable at all (no config files beyond `.gitignore`). A caller invoking the write path in a loop would be bounded only by the Access file's own 2 GB limit and its tendency to corrupt.
findings.gap: There is no way to cap the blast radius of a caller executing correct-but-catastrophic logic — e.g. inserting thousands of customer rows into a file store that corrupts under write pressure.
findings.recommendation: Implement per-principal business transaction limits (max records created per run/hour, max bulk operation size) in the service layer from API-Q1, configurable independently of request-rate throttling.

findings.title: Draft/Pending State
findings.description: There is no draft or pending state. The `Customers` insert in `cmdSave_Click` (frmCustomer.frm lines 25-27) writes `Name`, `CreatedBy`, `CreatedOn` only — no status column, no state machine, and no two-step create-then-confirm pattern. The write is committed immediately on button click with no reviewable intermediate record.
findings.gap: Every write is immediately final, so a proposed change cannot be staged for human review before it becomes authoritative data.
findings.recommendation: Add a status field (e.g. `PENDING_REVIEW` / `ACTIVE`) and a confirm operation so agent-proposed records land in a reviewable state before becoming live.

findings.title: Configurable Approval Gates
findings.description: No approval gate mechanism exists. `cmdSave_Click` executes the insert directly (frmCustomer.frm line 29) with no confirmation step, no approval endpoint, and no operation-level configuration flag — the application has no configuration surface at all. The only prompt in the code is a post-failure `MsgBox` (line 31), not a pre-execution approval.
findings.gap: High-risk operations cannot be configured to require human approval at the application layer, so there is no defense-in-depth beneath whatever gate the orchestration layer provides.
findings.recommendation: Make write operations approval-gated per operation type in the service layer from API-Q1 (request → approve → execute), so approval cannot be bypassed by calling the data layer directly.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Classification
findings.description: Stage A = Yes: `has_persistent_data_store` is true and the store holds customer business records — `frmCustomer.frm` writes a `Customers` table with `Name`, `CreatedBy`, `CreatedOn` (lines 25-27) into `S:\CRM\sales.mdb` (line 7), and README.md describes the system as a 'Sales CRM' whose Access file is the system of record for the field sales team. Customer names and the operator's Windows username are personal data. Stage B — B1: there is no response-scoping layer of any kind; the only integration path is full Jet/OLEDB access to the .mdb file (lines 19-21), which grants every column of every table to any caller holding `DB_PW`. No projections, DTOs, serializer exclusions, or field-level authorization exist. B2: no access-control differentiation — a single shared password is the whole authorization model (line 8). B3: no classification metadata — no tags, field annotations, data catalog, or PII tooling anywhere in the repository.
findings.gap: Agent-facing access is unscoped at every layer: no field filtering (B1), no sensitive-vs-non-sensitive access differentiation (B2), and no classification metadata (B3). A caller granted access to create a customer necessarily has read access to the entire CRM dataset.
findings.recommendation: Front the data with a service that returns explicit field projections, split permissions by data domain, and classify the customer fields; no caller should hold direct .mdb credentials.

findings.title: Data Residency and Sovereignty
findings.description: The system holds persistent customer data (`has_persistent_data_store` = true) in `S:\CRM\sales.mdb` on an SMB share (frmCustomer.frm line 7) with a nightly copy into a SQL Server 2012 reporting database (README.md). No residency or sovereignty control or statement exists anywhere in the repository: searched README.md, `.gitignore`, and `frmCustomer.frm` for GDPR/LGPD/HIPAA references, region-specific storage configuration, cross-region replication settings, and data sovereignty policy — zero results. The physical location of the file server and the reporting database is undocumented, and there is no IaC to pin it.
findings.gap: The jurisdiction of the customer data is undetermined and unconstrained, and there is no technical control preventing data read from the .mdb from being transmitted to an out-of-region processor (including an LLM endpoint).
findings.recommendation: Determine and document the residency requirements for the CRM customer dataset, record the authoritative storage location, and pin processing (including any LLM endpoint) to a compliant region before any agent reads this data.

findings.title: PII Redaction in Logs
findings.description: There is no redaction mechanism and no logging discipline. The system holds customer personal data (`has_persistent_data_store` = true, `Customers` table with `Name` and `CreatedBy`, frmCustomer.frm lines 25-27) but has no structured logging, no log scrubbing middleware, no PII masking utility, and no CloudWatch/Macie filters — searched the full repository (3 tracked files) for any logging framework or masking pattern with zero results. The only error surface is a `MsgBox` dialog (line 31). `.gitignore` excludes `*.log`, which indicates log files are produced somewhere in the operational process but no content control governs them; the full SQL statement — including the customer name — is held in the `sql` variable and would appear verbatim in any debugger, crash dump, or future log statement.
findings.gap: No redaction control exists for a system that handles customer PII, so any future or operational logging (including crash dumps and the nightly sync job) carries unmasked personal data into observable surfaces.
findings.recommendation: Introduce structured logging with an explicit PII allowlist/masking layer before adding any diagnostic logging to this write path, and confirm the nightly DTS/SSIS sync does not log row contents.

findings.title: Documented API Interface
findings.description: The repository contains only two server-rendered CFML pages. index.cfm emits an HTML table of documents and download.cfm streams a file with <cfcontent>. No REST, GraphQL, gRPC or AsyncAPI surface exists: searched for *.graphql/*.gql, openapi.*/swagger.*, *.smithy, AsyncAPI specs, and for any CFC component or remote-method declaration (access="remote", <cfcomponent>, <cffunction returnformat="json">) across all 4 repository files — zero results. The only machine-consumable integration paths are HTML scraping of index.cfm or direct SQL Server access to the docportal datasource.
findings.gap: There is no programmatic API for an agent to bind to. Integration would require UI scraping of HTML generated by index.cfm (fragile, non-auditable) or direct database access that bypasses the application's session check entirely.
findings.recommendation: Expose the document search and retrieval operations behind an HTTP JSON API — either by adding ColdFusion remote CFCs (access="remote", returnformat="json") in front of the existing queries as a tactical step, or preferably by extracting the document search/download operations into a supported runtime fronted by API Gateway. Publish an OpenAPI description of that surface (see API-Q2).

findings.title: Machine Identity Authentication
findings.description: Authentication is entirely human-session based. index.cfm declares <cfapplication sessionmanagement="yes" sessiontimeout="30 min"> and gates access with structKeyExists(session, "userid"), redirecting to login.cfm when absent. There is no OAuth2 client-credentials flow, no API key handling, no mTLS configuration, no service-account definition and no gateway authorizer anywhere in the repository; the README confirms "Application-managed sessions, no SSO". download.cfm performs no authentication check at all — it will stream any document to any unauthenticated caller that knows a doc_id.
findings.gap: There is no way for a non-human caller to authenticate as itself, and therefore no authenticated principal that could be attributed to an agent in any log. An agent could only integrate by replaying a human user's session cookie, which destroys attribution and inherits that human's full access.
findings.recommendation: Introduce machine identity before any agent integration: front the new API surface (API-Q1) with an identity provider issuing per-agent client credentials (OAuth 2.0 client-credentials or a gateway authorizer with per-key principal attribution), require the authenticated principal on every request including the download path, and carry that principal into the audit record (AUTH-Q6).

findings.title: Scoped Permissions (Least Privilege)
findings.description: Authorization is a single binary gate: index.cfm checks only whether session.userid exists, and every authenticated session sees the same unfiltered document list (the <cfquery> on lines 22-28 filters only on the title search term, never on the caller). download.cfm has no check whatsoever. There are no roles, groups, scopes or permission tables, and no IaC with IAM policies. All database access flows through the single shared "docportal" datasource.
findings.gap: The authorization model offers no mechanism to scope a caller down — a document-reading agent would necessarily receive the same access as every human user, across every document category, with unbounded blast radius.
findings.recommendation: Add a permission model keyed on the caller principal (minimum: per-category or per-document-owner access rules enforced inside the query predicate) so an agent identity can be granted access to a narrow document subset, and enforce it in both the listing and the download path.

findings.title: Action-Level Authorization
findings.description: No action-level authorization exists. The only check in the codebase is the session-existence test in index.cfm lines 5-7; there are no canRead/canWrite/canDelete style checks, no RBAC or ABAC policy definitions, no permission matrix, and no per-operation gating. Access to download.cfm is not distinguished from access to the listing page in any way.
findings.gap: The system cannot grant read without implicitly granting whatever other operations the application exposes (including the upload path documented in the README), so an agent's capability set cannot be constrained by action.
findings.recommendation: Define explicit operations (searchDocuments, downloadDocument, uploadDocument) and authorize each one separately against the caller principal, so a read-only agent identity is structurally incapable of invoking the write operations.

findings.title: Credential Management
findings.description: Database credentials are managed outside version control in the ColdFusion Administrator datasource definition (<cfquery datasource="docportal"> in both index.cfm and download.cfm references it by name), with no secrets manager and no rotation. The README discloses the administrator password in plaintext: "Datasource credentials configured in CF Administrator, password is 'cfadmin'". No aws_secretsmanager_* resources, Vault client, or .env file exist (.gitignore does exclude .env and .env.*).
findings.gap: A weak, documented, never-rotated administrator credential is recorded in the repository itself. Any caller — including an agent with access to repository content or to the README — can read it, and there is no rotation path that would limit the exposure window.
findings.recommendation: Rotate the ColdFusion Administrator password immediately and remove the plaintext value from README.md and from git history. Move the datasource credential into a managed secret store with scheduled rotation, and grant the application a least-privilege SQL login (SELECT on dbo.documents only) rather than an administrative one.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: No audit logging exists. Neither index.cfm nor download.cfm writes any log record — there is no <cflog>, no Application.cfc, no CloudTrail or CloudWatch configuration (no IaC of any kind), and no immutable or tamper-evident log storage. Document retrievals through download.cfm leave no trace of who retrieved which document. agent_scope resolved to read-only, so this is RISK-SAFETY rather than BLOCKER.
findings.gap: There is no record attributing any access to a principal, so agent-initiated document retrievals would be indistinguishable from human ones and entirely invisible after the fact — forensics on a document exfiltration would be impossible.
findings.recommendation: Emit a structured access log for every search and download containing the authenticated principal (AUTH-Q1), the document id, the timestamp and the caller type, and ship it to append-only storage with retention and integrity validation enabled.

findings.title: Agent Identity Suspension
findings.description: There is no identity to suspend and no mechanism to suspend one. The repository contains no API key store, no credential revocation endpoint, no service-account disable path and no IAM/Cognito configuration. The only revocation primitive implied by the code is ColdFusion session expiry (sessiontimeout 30 minutes in index.cfm line 3), which is time-based and cannot be targeted at a single misbehaving caller.
findings.gap: A misbehaving integration could only be stopped by taking the application offline or by changing the shared datasource credential — both of which disrupt every user. Per-identity isolation is not possible.
findings.recommendation: Issue per-agent credentials through an identity provider that supports immediate revocation, and verify that disabling one agent credential leaves human sessions and other integrations unaffected.

findings.title: Compensation and Rollback
findings.description: No transactional or compensating logic exists. Both pages issue single standalone <cfquery> SELECT statements with no <cftransaction> wrapper, no saga or two-phase pattern, and no undo operation. download.cfm streams from the local filesystem with deletefile="no". The README notes documents live on local disk "D:\docroot\files (no object storage, no backups offsite)" on a single instance, so there is also no restore path if state is lost. agent_scope resolved to read-only, so the conditional BLOCKER resolves to RISK-SAFETY.
findings.gap: The system has no compensation primitive at all. The read paths present today need none, but the documented upload path writes to a single local disk with no backup, meaning any state damage is unrecoverable rather than compensable.
findings.recommendation: Before any write-enabled integration, wrap multi-step document operations in explicit transactions, move document bytes to durable versioned object storage so a bad write can be rolled back to a prior version, and define an explicit undo operation for upload and delete.

findings.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
findings.description: No rate limiting exists at any layer reachable from this repository. There is no IaC (no API Gateway throttle, no WAF rate rule), no middleware, and no application-level counter in index.cfm or download.cfm. Every request to index.cfm executes an unbounded LIKE '%...%' scan against dbo.documents, and every download.cfm request streams a file from local disk on the single Windows instance described in the README.
findings.gap: A looping caller can issue unbounded full-table LIKE scans and unbounded disk reads against a single-instance SQL Server 2005 backend with no throttle, which will degrade or exhaust the server for all users.
findings.recommendation: Place the agent-facing surface behind a gateway enforcing per-principal request throttling, and add a server-side result cap and query timeout so a single caller cannot monopolise the database.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Classification
findings.description: Stage A = Yes: the application owns a persistent SQL Server store (datasource "docportal", table dbo.documents) holding internal policy documents and forms plus user-attribution fields (uploaded_by, uploaded_on), and the README describes it as an intranet portal for policy documents and forms. Stage B — B1 is CLEAR: both queries use explicit column projections (index.cfm selects doc_id, title, category, uploaded_by, uploaded_on; download.cfm selects filename only) and no credential or secret column is returned to callers. B2 FIRES: there is no access differentiation whatsoever — a single session-existence check grants every caller the complete document list regardless of category, and download.cfm applies no check at all, so no scope separates sensitive document categories from routine ones. B3 is ABSENT: no classification tags, no field-level sensitivity annotations, no Macie/Presidio integration and no documented classification policy exist anywhere in the repository.
findings.gap: No access-control differentiation exists between sensitive and non-sensitive document categories (B2), and no formal classification metadata identifies which documents are sensitive (B3). An agent granted document read access necessarily receives every document in the store, including any HR, legal or financial material filed in it.
findings.recommendation: Classify the document categories already present in the category column, then enforce category-scoped access per caller principal in both the listing predicate and the download handler so an agent identity can be restricted to non-sensitive categories. Record the classification as queryable metadata rather than convention.

findings.title: Data Residency and Sovereignty
findings.description: The system holds a persistent data store (SQL Server 2005 via the docportal datasource) and document bytes on local disk at D:\docroot\files per the README. No residency or sovereignty controls or statements were found: the repository contains no IaC with region constraints, no cross-region replication configuration, and no GDPR/LGPD/HIPAA references in README.md or either CFML page. agent_scope resolved to read-only, so the conditional BLOCKER resolves to RISK-SAFETY.
findings.gap: The jurisdictional constraints on the document corpus are undocumented, so there is no basis on which to decide whether document contents may be transmitted to an LLM endpoint in another region. Document bodies are streamed verbatim by download.cfm, meaning full file contents — not just metadata — would cross whatever boundary the agent runtime sits behind.
findings.recommendation: Determine and document the residency classification of the document corpus before any agent consumes document bodies, pin the agent runtime and model endpoint to an approved region, and record the constraint alongside the document category classification from DATA-Q1.

findings.title: PII Redaction in Logs
findings.description: No log redaction is possible because no logging layer exists to redact in: there is no <cflog>, no Application.cfc, no log scrubbing middleware, no CloudWatch filter and no Macie integration. Failures instead fall through to default ColdFusion 8 error pages, which render the failing query text and request scope — and since url.q is interpolated into the SQL on index.cfm line 26 and session.fullname is rendered on line 15, user-supplied search terms and user names are present in the data that an unhandled exception page would display. The README confirms the application runs over plain HTTP on the internal network, so that output is also unencrypted in transit.
findings.gap: User search terms and user identities reach error output through an uncontrolled path, with no redaction, no structured logging to apply redaction to, and no control over who sees the resulting error pages.
findings.recommendation: Disable detailed ColdFusion error output in production and add an Application.cfc onError handler that logs a structured record with user-supplied values redacted, then apply an allowlist to the fields written to the access log once logging is introduced (AUTH-Q6).

findings.title: Documented API Interface
findings.description: The repository exposes only server-rendered Django 1.4 views. `tickets/views.py` defines two function views: `ticket_list` returns an HTML template render (`render_to_response('tickets/list.html', ...)`) and `ticket_search` returns a hand-concatenated HTML `<ul>` string via `HttpResponse`. Searched for REST/GraphQL/AsyncAPI surfaces across all 4 repository files: no DRF (`rest_framework`) in `INSTALLED_APPS` in helpdesk/settings.py, no `@api_view`/serializers, no GraphQL schema files (`.graphql`/`.gql`), no AsyncAPI or Smithy models, no dependency manifest declaring an API framework.
findings.gap: There is no machine-consumable API. An agent integrating with this system today would have to scrape HTML or connect directly to PostgreSQL ('helpdesk' database, 127.0.0.1:5432 per helpdesk/settings.py) — both brittle, unauditable coupling patterns.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a versioned JSON API in front of the ticket data (e.g., Django REST Framework `/api/v1/tickets` with list/detail endpoints) as the single agent integration surface, and keep the HTML views as a separate presentation layer. Do not expose the database directly to agents.

findings.title: Machine Identity Authentication
findings.description: Only human session authentication is configured. helpdesk/settings.py installs `django.contrib.auth`, `django.contrib.sessions` and `AuthenticationMiddleware` — cookie/session based login for people. Searched all files for OAuth2 client-credentials flows, API-key authentication with principal attribution, mTLS configuration, service-account definitions, Cognito app clients, and gateway authorizers: none found. Neither view in tickets/views.py reads `request.user` or any caller identity.
findings.gap: There is no machine identity an agent could use, and no mechanism to attribute a call to a specific non-human principal. Every downstream authorization and audit decision (AUTH-Q2, AUTH-Q3, AUTH-Q6) is therefore unenforceable.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a machine-identity path for the new API layer: OAuth 2.0 client credentials (or per-agent API keys issued from a managed store) where each agent gets a distinct principal ID that is carried into request context and logs.

findings.title: Scoped Permissions (Least Privilege)
findings.description: No authorization scoping exists. `ticket_list` and `ticket_search` in tickets/views.py have no `@login_required`, no permission decorator, and no permission check in the body — they execute raw SQL for any caller that can reach the URL. helpdesk/settings.py installs `django.contrib.auth` (which provides a permission model) and `django.contrib.admin`, but no group, permission, or per-caller scope is defined anywhere in the repository, and no IaC/IAM policies exist to scope access at the platform layer.
findings.gap: All authorization is effectively coarse-grained: any caller reaching the endpoint receives the full ticket result set, so an agent identity cannot be granted a narrowed slice.
findings.recommendation: Define Django permissions/groups (or API-key scopes) for ticket read access and enforce them in the API layer, granting agent principals only the minimum ticket fields and rows required.

findings.title: Action-Level Authorization
findings.description: No action-level authorization is implemented. There are no `canRead`/`canWrite`/`canDelete` style checks, no ABAC/RBAC matrix, and no method-level gating in tickets/views.py; Django's default admin (django.contrib.admin in helpdesk/settings.py) grants full model access to staff users without any agent-specific differentiation.
findings.gap: The system cannot express 'read tickets but never delete them' for an agent principal — a prerequisite for any mixed read/write agent workflow.
findings.recommendation: Implement per-action permission checks (`tickets.view_ticket`, `tickets.change_ticket`, `tickets.delete_ticket`) enforced in the API layer and assign only view permissions to agent principals.

findings.title: Credential Management
findings.description: Credentials are hardcoded in source control. helpdesk/settings.py contains the PostgreSQL password in plaintext (`'PASSWORD': 'helpdesk2012'`) and a committed Django `SECRET_KEY` (`'x9d2#kf!3v_legacy_secret_do_not_change_2012'`); README.md explicitly acknowledges 'SECRET_KEY committed to settings.py'. Searched for Secrets Manager / Vault / SSM usage and environment-variable indirection: `import os` is present but never used for credentials, and no secrets-management client appears anywhere in the repository.
findings.gap: No secrets manager, no rotation, and no environment indirection. Any repository reader obtains database access, and the static SECRET_KEY allows session/signature forgery. Prompt-injection or a verbose error path could surface these values to an agent.
findings.recommendation: Move both values to a secrets store (AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store) read via environment variables at startup, rotate the database password and SECRET_KEY, and purge the values from git history.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: There is no audit logging of callers. The only logging in the codebase is a debug statement — `print "searching tickets for:", q` in `ticket_search` (tickets/views.py) — which records the query text but no principal, timestamp, or outcome. Searched for CloudTrail, log-file validation, S3 Object Lock, and CloudWatch retention configuration: no IaC of any kind exists in the repository. Deployment is a manual `git pull` plus Apache restart per README.md, so logs are local Apache/stdout files on one EC2 instance.
findings.gap: No principal attribution, no tamper-evident storage, and no retention policy. Agent-initiated reads would be indistinguishable from human traffic, and any log that does exist is mutable on the host.
findings.recommendation: Emit structured access logs including the authenticated machine principal, ship them off-host to CloudWatch Logs with a retention policy, and store archived copies in an S3 bucket with Object Lock for tamper evidence.

findings.title: Agent Identity Suspension
findings.description: No revocation mechanism exists. Because there are no API keys, service accounts, or agent identities (AUTH-Q1), there is nothing to suspend. The only identity lifecycle available is disabling a Django user via django.contrib.admin, which requires a human account and does not isolate a machine caller.
findings.gap: A misbehaving agent could only be stopped by blocking it at the network layer or taking the single Apache instance down — which also removes service for all human users.
findings.recommendation: Issue per-agent credentials that can be individually disabled (API key deactivation or IAM/IdP client disable) and document a revocation runbook that does not require a service restart.

findings.title: Compensation and Rollback
findings.description: No compensation or rollback capability is present. tickets/views.py uses `connection.cursor()` for direct SQL reads with no transaction management (`transaction.atomic` / `commit_on_success` do not appear), no saga or compensating-action code, and no undo endpoints. There are no multi-step write workflows in the repository to compensate for, but there is also no mechanism available if writes are added.
findings.gap: The codebase has no transactional envelope at all, so a future multi-step agent workflow would leave partial state with no recovery path.
findings.recommendation: Wrap any future multi-step write path in an explicit database transaction and expose compensating operations (e.g., ticket status revert) before enabling write-capable agents.

findings.title: Circuit Breakers and Resilience
findings.description: No resilience controls protect the system's own dependencies. It calls PostgreSQL (helpdesk/settings.py DATABASES) and an on-prem SMTP relay at `exchange.acme-corp.internal:25`. Searched for retry logic, exponential backoff, circuit breakers, and timeout configuration: none present — `connection.cursor()` calls in tickets/views.py are unguarded, and no `EMAIL_TIMEOUT` or connection timeout is configured.
findings.gap: A slow or unavailable PostgreSQL or Exchange relay causes requests to hang on Apache's worker threads with no circuit breaker, so agent-speed traffic can exhaust the single instance and cascade failures back to the caller.
findings.recommendation: Set explicit database and SMTP timeouts, add bounded retry with backoff around the external relay, and add a circuit breaker (or a queue for email) so dependency latency cannot consume all request workers.

findings.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
findings.description: No rate limiting exists at any layer. helpdesk/settings.py MIDDLEWARE_CLASSES contains only CommonMiddleware, SessionMiddleware and AuthenticationMiddleware — no `django-ratelimit` or throttling middleware. No API Gateway, WAF, or usage-plan IaC exists in the repository, and README.md describes a single Apache 2.2 + mod_wsgi EC2 instance with the database on the same box.
findings.gap: A runaway agent loop would hit unbounded raw-SQL queries (including the unindexed `LIKE '%...%'` search in tickets/views.py) on a co-located PostgreSQL instance, taking down the app and its database together.
findings.recommendation: Add per-principal throttling in front of the agent-facing API (gateway usage plan or django-ratelimit) with a conservative requests-per-minute ceiling for agent keys.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Classification
findings.description: Stage A = Yes: the system stores user-specific helpdesk data — `tickets_ticket` carries `requester`, `subject`, `priority` and `status` (queried in tickets/views.py), and `has_logging_of_user_data` is true because `ticket_search` prints the user-supplied query string. Stage B results: B1 is CLEAR — both queries use explicit column projections (`SELECT id, subject, requester, priority` and `SELECT id, subject`) and no credential or password column is exposed; Django auth tables are not surfaced by either view. B2 FIRES — there is no access-control differentiation whatsoever: no permission checks in the views, no scopes, no row- or column-level security, so a single reachable URL grants access to all ticket content including requester identity and free-text subjects. B3 is absent — no classification tags, field-level sensitivity annotations, or PII-detection tooling (Macie/Presidio) appear in the repository.
findings.gap: Sensitive-field exclusion happens only incidentally through hand-written SELECT lists, and no access tier separates general ticket metadata from requester-identifying or free-text content. Formal classification metadata is absent (B3, INFO).
findings.recommendation: Introduce at least two access tiers for ticket data (metadata-only vs. full content including `requester` and `subject`) enforced in the API layer, and annotate requester/subject as sensitive fields so projections are deliberate rather than incidental.

findings.title: Data Residency and Sovereignty
findings.description: The system holds persistent user data in PostgreSQL (helpdesk/settings.py) and logs user-submitted search text (tickets/views.py), so residency constraints are in scope. Searched for residency or sovereignty signals: README.md documents a single EC2 instance with a co-located PostgreSQL 9.1 and an on-prem Exchange relay but states no jurisdiction; there are no GDPR/LGPD references, no region-pinning configuration, and no cross-region replication settings. The only locality signal in the codebase is `TIME_ZONE = 'America/New_York'`.
findings.gap: Residency obligations for internal helpdesk tickets (which can contain employee-identifying content) are undocumented, so there is no basis to decide whether ticket content may be sent to an LLM endpoint in another region.
findings.recommendation: Document the data classification and permitted processing jurisdictions for ticket content, and pin agent/LLM inference to an approved region before any ticket text leaves the current environment.

findings.title: PII Redaction in Logs
findings.description: User-submitted content is written to logs unredacted and error output is verbose. `ticket_search` executes `print "searching tickets for:", q` (tickets/views.py) — the raw search string, which in a helpdesk context routinely contains employee names, email addresses, and account details — and under mod_wsgi stdout lands in the Apache error log. `DEBUG = True` in helpdesk/settings.py causes Django to render full tracebacks including local variables and query parameters. Searched for log scrubbing middleware, PII masking utilities, CloudWatch log filters, or Macie integration: none found.
findings.gap: There is no redaction layer, so PII entered into search queries and present in exception context is persisted to host log files with no retention or access control.
findings.recommendation: Remove the debug `print`, set `DEBUG = False`, route logging through Django's logging framework with a redaction filter for free-text and identifier fields, and restrict and expire the resulting log storage.

findings.title: Documented API Interface
findings.description: The only callable surface is a Struts 1 HTML form action: struts-config.xml maps path '/loan' to com.acme.loan.LoanAction with forwards to quote.jsp and confirm.jsp. No REST controller, GraphQL schema, AsyncAPI spec or RPC service exists anywhere in the repository (searched for @RestController/@Path/servlet REST mappings, *.graphql, *.smithy, openapi.*/swagger.*). Integration therefore requires HTML form posting and JSP screen scraping, or direct Oracle access using the credentials embedded in LoanAction.java.
findings.gap: No machine-callable API. The business logic (amortization calculation and application submission) is only reachable through a browser-oriented Struts action bound to JSP views.
findings.recommendation: Extract the pricing and submission logic from LoanAction.execute into a service class and expose it over a documented JSON/HTTP API (or a facade service in front of the WAR) so agent tools bind to a contract rather than to JSP markup.

findings.title: Idempotent Write Operations
findings.description: The submit path performs an unconditional INSERT INTO applications in saveApplication with no idempotency key, no natural-key uniqueness check and no read-before-write. A repeated submit (agent retry or duplicate tool call) creates a second loan application row. The action is dispatched purely on the form value 'submit' (lf.getAction()).
findings.gap: No idempotency mechanism exists for the only write operation in the system.
findings.recommendation: Accept a caller-supplied idempotency key, persist it with a unique constraint on the applications table, and return the original result on replay.

findings.title: Machine Identity Authentication
findings.description: The application reads request.getRemoteUser() and stores it as the 'officer' column, which implies container-managed (WebLogic) human login, but no authentication configuration exists in the repository: there is no web.xml, no login-config, no security-constraint, no OAuth/mTLS/API-key handling, and no service account definition. The only credential in the repo is a shared Oracle account (DB_USER='loan_app') hardcoded in LoanAction.java.
findings.gap: No machine identity mechanism and no principal attribution for non-human callers; an agent could only call the system by impersonating a loan officer's interactive session.
findings.recommendation: Front the extracted API with an authenticating gateway issuing per-agent client credentials (OAuth2 client_credentials or mTLS), and carry the agent principal through to the persisted record and logs.

findings.title: Scoped Permissions (Least Privilege)
findings.description: There is no authorization model in the repository: no role checks, no permission matrix, no IAM/IaC policies (no .tf/.yaml/CloudFormation present). All database access uses one shared Oracle account 'loan_app' declared in LoanAction.java, so every caller inherits identical, full table privileges.
findings.gap: No mechanism to grant a caller read-only or narrowed access — authorization is entirely coarse-grained.
findings.recommendation: Introduce per-caller scopes at the API gateway and distinct database roles (read-only vs insert) so an agent identity can be granted the minimum needed.

findings.title: Action-Level Authorization
findings.description: LoanAction.execute branches on the client-supplied form field lf.getAction(): any caller that reaches the action can trigger the submit (INSERT) path. There is no canRead/canWrite check, no roles attribute on the action mapping in struts-config.xml, and no method-level authorization.
findings.gap: Quote (read-like) and submit (write) operations are indistinguishable from an authorization standpoint — a caller permitted to price a loan is implicitly permitted to create one.
findings.recommendation: Split quote and submit into separately authorized operations and enforce the write permission server-side, not via a form field.

findings.title: Identity Propagation and Delegation
findings.description: The only identity handling is request.getRemoteUser() passed as a string into the SQL INSERT. There is no JWT/OAuth parsing, no token exchange, no on-behalf-of flow, and no way to distinguish a caller acting as itself from a caller acting for a loan officer — the officer field is simply whatever the container reports.
findings.gap: An agent acting on behalf of a loan officer cannot be bounded by that officer's permissions, and the audit column cannot separate actor from subject.
findings.recommendation: Propagate a verified token to the service layer and persist both the acting principal (agent) and the subject principal (officer) on every application record.

findings.title: Credential Management
findings.description: Production Oracle credentials are hardcoded as constants in source: DB_URL='jdbc:oracle:thin:@dbprod01:1521:LOANDB', DB_USER='loan_app', DB_PASS='loanApp2010' in LoanAction.java, with a comment noting they are also duplicated in db.properties inside the WAR (README: 'Connection details in a properties file inside the WAR'). No secrets manager, Vault, or rotation mechanism is referenced anywhere.
findings.gap: A static, unrotated production database password is committed to version control and duplicated in the deployment artifact — exactly the kind of secret an agent-facing surface or prompt-injection path can exfiltrate.
findings.recommendation: Move the credential to a managed secret store with rotation, obtain connections from a WebLogic/JNDI datasource instead of DriverManager, remove the constants, and rotate the 'loan_app' password since it is already exposed in git history.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: The only record of a write is the business row itself: the INSERT stores the 'officer' value in the applications table. There is no application log statement in LoanAction.java at all, no logging framework dependency, and no immutable or tamper-evident log store (no CloudTrail/object-lock/retention configuration — the repo contains no IaC). The audit field is in the same mutable table the application writes to.
findings.gap: No immutable, attributable audit trail for loan application creation — a regulated financial write. Forensics on an agent-initiated submission would be impossible.
findings.recommendation: Emit a structured audit event per write (principal, operation, parameters, timestamp, correlation id) to an append-only store with retention, independent of the applications table.

findings.title: Agent Identity Suspension
findings.description: No identity lifecycle controls exist: no API key store or revocation endpoint, no service account definitions, and the single database identity is a hardcoded shared account. Disabling a misbehaving caller would mean changing the shared 'loan_app' password or undeploying the WAR, which stops all users.
findings.gap: No way to suspend one caller without taking down the whole application.
findings.recommendation: Issue per-agent credentials at the gateway so an individual identity can be revoked independently of the application deployment.

findings.title: Compensation and Rollback
findings.description: saveApplication opens a connection with DriverManager.getConnection (default autocommit), executes a single string-built INSERT, and closes. There is no transaction boundary, no rollback in a catch/finally block (the connection is not even closed on failure), no compensating 'cancel application' operation, and no saga/undo pattern. The submit path also mutates the form (setMonthlyPayment) before writing.
findings.gap: A partially completed or erroneous submission cannot be undone through any supported operation; there is no reversal endpoint and no transactional rollback on failure.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the write in an explicit transaction with rollback and close resources in finally (or try-with-resources after a JDK upgrade), and add an explicit cancel/void operation so an agent-initiated submission can be compensated.

findings.title: Concurrency Controls
findings.description: No concurrency control exists: the INSERT carries no version column, no conditional predicate and no SELECT FOR UPDATE, and no ETag/If-Match handling is present. README explicitly records the known defect 'ActionForms hold mutable shared state; thread-safety bugs under load', and LoanAction's own header comment warns 'Struts 1 Actions are singletons - keep all state local'.
findings.gap: Concurrent callers can interleave on shared mutable form state and create duplicate or inconsistent application rows; the documented thread-safety defect is amplified by machine-speed concurrency.
findings.recommendation: Add optimistic locking (version column / If-Match) on mutable records and verify the Action holds no instance state before allowing concurrent agent callers.

findings.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
findings.description: No throttling exists at any layer present in the repository: no rate-limiting servlet filter, no gateway or WAF configuration (no IaC at all), and the HTTP surface is the raw Struts action mapped in struts-config.xml. Each submit also opens a brand-new Oracle connection via DriverManager, so unthrottled calls translate directly into database session pressure.
findings.gap: A runaway agent loop can exhaust WebLogic threads and Oracle sessions, taking down the loan origination path for human officers.
findings.recommendation: Enforce request-rate limits in front of the application (gateway or filter) and use a bounded JNDI connection pool instead of per-request DriverManager connections.

findings.title: Blast Radius and Transaction Limits
findings.description: No business-domain limits exist. There is no per-caller cap on applications submitted, no principal or APR ceiling enforced in code (the header comment references a 2017 'APR cap' change, but execute() applies no cap — it computes payment from the submitted rate with no bounds), and no bulk-operation or spend threshold.
findings.gap: The business impact of an erroneous agent loop is unbounded: it could submit an unlimited number of loan applications at arbitrary principal and rate values.
findings.recommendation: Enforce configurable per-caller business limits (applications per hour, maximum principal, allowed APR range) in the service layer, independent of request-rate limiting.

findings.title: Draft/Pending State
findings.description: The submit path commits immediately: saveApplication inserts the application row with columns (applicant, principal, rate, term, officer) and no status column, and the action then forwards to confirm.jsp. There is no draft/pending state, no two-step create-then-confirm API, and no approval status in the schema implied by the INSERT.
findings.gap: An agent cannot propose a loan application for human review — any write it makes is final on first call.
findings.recommendation: Add a status column with a PENDING/DRAFT state, have agent-initiated writes land in PENDING, and require an explicit confirm operation to finalize.

findings.title: Configurable Approval Gates
findings.description: No approval mechanism exists: struts-config.xml exposes a single action with two forwards, there is no approval endpoint, no per-operation configuration flag, and no workflow engine. 'confirm' is a JSP view shown after the write, not a gate before it.
findings.gap: High-risk operations (loan submission) cannot be configured to require human approval at the application layer, so the only possible gate is outside the system.
findings.recommendation: Introduce per-operation approval configuration so submission by a non-human principal requires an explicit human approval call before the record becomes effective.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Classification
findings.description: Stage A = Yes: the system persists applicant PII and financial data — INSERT INTO applications (applicant, principal, rate, term, officer) in LoanAction.saveApplication, backed by Oracle 11g per README. Stage B1: there is no response scoping of any kind — no DTOs, no @JsonIgnore/write-only serialization, no column projection; the form object LoanForm carries applicant name, principal and computed payment and is handed directly to JSP views. Stage B2: access control is a single shared database account ('loan_app') with no scope differentiation between sensitive and non-sensitive data. Stage B3: no classification metadata — no field-level sensitivity annotations, no tags (no IaC), no Macie/Presidio tooling.
findings.gap: Agent-facing access to applicant PII and loan financials is unscoped and undifferentiated, and the data carries no classification metadata.
findings.recommendation: Define response DTOs that expose only the fields an agent needs, split database privileges so PII-bearing columns require a distinct scope, and annotate applicant fields as PII in the schema and code.

findings.title: Data Residency and Sovereignty
findings.description: The system stores loan applicant PII and financial terms in Oracle 11g on a Solaris host in a single data center (README Architecture section), yet the repository contains no residency or sovereignty controls or documentation: no GDPR/LGPD/jurisdiction references, no region configuration, no cross-border transfer policy, and no data-handling statement. The connection target is a bare hostname (dbprod01) with no region semantics.
findings.gap: Residency constraints on regulated consumer-lending PII are undocumented and unenforced, so there is nothing preventing an agent from forwarding that data to an LLM endpoint in another jurisdiction.
findings.recommendation: Document the jurisdiction and applicable regime for the applications dataset, and enforce an allowed-region/processor policy for any agent or LLM integration that reads it.

findings.title: PII Redaction in Logs
findings.description: There is no logging framework and no log statement in the codebase (no log4j/commons-logging/SLF4J usage in LoanAction.java, no logging configuration file), and consequently no scrubbing or masking layer. Failures instead propagate: execute() and saveApplication() both declare 'throws Exception', so JDBC exceptions escape to the WebLogic container. Because the SQL is built by string concatenation, the exception message carries the fully interpolated statement including the applicant name, which lands unredacted in container logs. .gitignore excludes *.log, so no sample log is available to inspect.
findings.gap: No redaction control exists on the one path that does emit user data — stack traces and SQL text containing applicant PII reach container logs in the clear.
findings.recommendation: Introduce structured logging with an explicit PII masking/allowlist policy, catch JDBC exceptions and log a sanitized message without the SQL text or applicant values.

findings.title: Documented API Interface
findings.description: The only integration surface is a single SOAP 1.1 RPC/encoded operation, submitOrder(partnerId, poXml), declared in the hand-maintained WSDL at wsdl/PurchaseOrderService.wsdl and implemented in src/com/acme/partner/PurchaseOrderService.java. No REST, GraphQL, or AsyncAPI surface exists. The business payload is passed as an opaque xsd:string (poXml) whose structure is documented nowhere in the repository - the implementation reads poNumber and amount by getElementsByTagName, and no XSD for the purchase-order document is present.
findings.gap: There is no machine-consumable description of the actual request payload. An agent cannot construct a valid call from the WSDL alone because the WSDL types the payload as a bare string. README.md states the WSDL is hand-edited and drifts from the implementation, so even the operation signature is not a trustworthy contract.
findings.recommendation: Publish an explicit schema for the purchase-order document (XSD, or a JSON schema behind a new REST/JSON facade) and generate the contract from the implementation rather than hand-editing it. The lowest-risk path is a thin JSON/REST or MCP-facing facade in front of submitOrder with a typed request body (partnerId, poNumber, amount, line items) so agents bind to named fields instead of an opaque XML blob.

findings.title: Idempotent Write Operations
findings.description: submitOrder performs an unconditional INSERT INTO partner_orders for every call (src/com/acme/partner/PurchaseOrderService.java lines 38-41). There is no idempotency key parameter in the WSDL message submitOrderRequest, no uniqueness check on po_number before insert, and no evidence of a unique constraint being relied on (the code never handles a duplicate-key path). Two identical calls create two orders.
findings.gap: No idempotency key support and no business-key deduplication on the single write operation. Agent retries - which are routine on timeout and common under LLM non-determinism - will duplicate purchase orders.
findings.recommendation: Add an idempotency key (or treat partnerId + poNumber as the business key) with a unique constraint on partner_orders, and return the original result on a repeat submission instead of inserting again.

findings.title: Machine Identity Authentication
findings.description: No authentication is implemented in the service. submitOrder accepts partnerId as an ordinary caller-supplied string parameter and uses it directly as the identity written to the database; nothing verifies that the caller is that partner. README.md describes the intended control as 'WS-Security username token, password sent in plaintext' with 'Partner credentials stored in a flat properties file', but no WS-Security handler, no JAX-WS handler chain, no deployment descriptor, and no properties file exist in the repository. There is no OAuth2 client-credentials flow, no mTLS configuration, no API key with principal attribution, and no gateway authorizer.
findings.gap: No verifiable machine identity. The authenticated principal is self-asserted by the caller, and even the documented mechanism (plaintext PasswordText over plain HTTP) cannot be used to attribute an agent identity safely. Every downstream authorization and audit decision is therefore unenforceable.
findings.recommendation: Front the endpoint with a modern machine-identity mechanism - OAuth 2.0 client credentials or mTLS per partner, terminated at a gateway - and derive partnerId from the authenticated principal instead of trusting the request parameter.

findings.title: Scoped Permissions (Least Privilege)
findings.description: There is one shared credential and no permission model. All callers execute through the single hardcoded Oracle account partner_app (DB_USER/DB_PASS constants, lines 22-23), and the single operation is available to anyone who can reach the endpoint. No IAM policies, no resource policies, no role definitions, and no per-partner permission configuration exist in the repository.
findings.gap: Authorization is entirely coarse-grained: there is no mechanism to grant an agent identity narrower access than 'may submit orders as any partner through the shared database account'. Scoping down an agent is not possible without new code.
findings.recommendation: Introduce per-caller scopes enforced at the gateway or in a JAX-WS handler (for example submit:order only), and separate database privileges from the application-wide shared account.

findings.title: Action-Level Authorization
findings.description: No authorization check of any kind appears in submitOrder - the method body goes straight from XML parsing to the INSERT. There are no canRead/canWrite/canDelete checks, no RBAC or ABAC definitions, no permission matrix, and no method-level authorization annotations (no @RolesAllowed, no interceptors). The WSDL exposes exactly one operation with no per-operation security policy.
findings.gap: The service cannot distinguish an agent permitted to read from one permitted to write; the only exposed action is a write and it is unguarded. Any future read or cancel operation would inherit the same absence.
findings.recommendation: Add per-operation authorization (declarative @RolesAllowed on the endpoint plus gateway method-level policy) keyed to the authenticated principal established by AUTH-Q1.

findings.title: Identity Propagation and Delegation
findings.description: No identity is propagated or distinguished. partnerId arrives as a @WebParam string and is written directly into partner_orders; there is no JWT parsing, no token exchange, no on-behalf-of flow, and no user-context header handling. The service cannot tell an agent acting as itself from an agent acting on behalf of a specific partner user, because it has no identity context at all beyond the string it is handed.
findings.gap: Agent-as-self and agent-on-behalf-of-partner are indistinguishable, and the subject of the operation (which partner the order is booked against) is attacker-controllable - a privilege-escalation path by construction.
findings.recommendation: Carry the caller identity as a signed token, derive the order's partner from that token, and record both actor (agent identity) and subject (partner) separately on each submission.

findings.title: Credential Management
findings.description: Database credentials are hardcoded in source: DB_URL = "jdbc:oracle:thin:@10.0.9.30:1521:PARTDB", DB_USER = "partner_app", DB_PASS = "partner2009" as private static final String constants. No secrets manager or Vault integration exists (searched for aws_secretsmanager_*, Vault clients, and any IaC - the repository has no infrastructure code at all). README.md additionally documents 'Partner credentials stored in a flat properties file' and WS-Security passwords sent in plaintext.
findings.gap: Credentials are committed to version control, shared, and unrotatable without a code change and redeploy. The password value is embedded in a compiled artifact, so rotation requires a release. This is severe evidence on a RISK-SAFETY question: a prompt-injection or error-leak path (see DATA-Q6) could expose the connection string.
findings.recommendation: Move the datasource to a JBoss/container-managed datasource backed by a secrets manager with rotation, remove the constants from source, and rotate the partner_app password immediately since it is exposed in git history.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: There is no logging at all in the write path. submitOrder contains no logger, no println, and no audit insert; the catch block swallows the exception into a returned string. No CloudTrail, no log-retention configuration, no object-locked log storage, and no immutable log store exist (the repository contains no IaC or configuration files beyond .gitignore). The only persisted trace of a write is the partner_orders row itself, which records a caller-supplied partner_id and no actor, timestamp, or request identifier.
findings.gap: No audit record of who submitted which order. An agent-submitted purchase order is indistinguishable from a human partner submission, and there is no tamper-evident log to support forensics or compliance evidence for financial records.
findings.recommendation: Emit a structured audit event for every submitOrder call (authenticated principal, agent identity, partnerId, poNumber, amount, outcome, correlation id) to an append-only store with retention and integrity validation.

findings.title: Agent Identity Suspension
findings.description: No identity lifecycle mechanism exists. There are no API keys to revoke, no IAM roles to disable, and no user store - README.md documents partner credentials living in 'a flat properties file' that is not even present in the repository, and onboarding as 'a manual SOAP-UI session'. Suspending one caller would require editing that file and, on JBoss AS 5.1, redeploying or restarting the application.
findings.gap: A misbehaving agent cannot be isolated quickly or selectively. The only available containment is taking the whole endpoint down, which also cuts off every legitimate partner.
findings.recommendation: Move partner/agent credentials into a managed identity store (gateway API keys, OAuth clients, or per-partner certificates) where a single identity can be disabled immediately without redeploying the service.

findings.title: Compensation and Rollback
findings.description: No transaction control and no compensation path. submitOrder obtains a raw DriverManager connection (line 38), executes a single executeUpdate in autocommit mode, and closes the statement and connection; there is no setAutoCommit(false), no commit/rollback, no @Transactional, no saga or compensating action, and no undo or cancel operation in the WSDL. If anything fails after the insert, the inserted order stays. If the connection leaks (the close calls are not in a finally block - an exception between lines 38 and 43 skips them), the order may be committed with no result returned to the caller.
findings.gap: There is no way to reverse an accepted purchase order through the API, and no transactional boundary around the write. An agent that times out after a successful insert has no way to determine or undo what happened - and no read operation exists to check (STATE-Q2).
findings.recommendation: Wrap the write in an explicit transaction with resources closed in finally (or try-with-resources), and expose a cancelOrder/reverseOrder operation so an agent-initiated submission can be compensated.

findings.title: Concurrency Controls
findings.description: No concurrency control exists. The insert is a bare Statement.executeUpdate with no version column, no ETag/If-Match handling, no SELECT FOR UPDATE, no conditional write, and no unique constraint referenced in code. Concurrent calls carrying the same poNumber will both succeed and create duplicate order rows.
findings.gap: Nothing prevents two concurrent agent instances (or an agent racing a human partner) from booking the same purchase order twice, and there is no conflict signal the agent could react to.
findings.recommendation: Enforce a unique business key on (partner_id, po_number) and return a distinguishable conflict fault, which gives agents a deterministic conflict signal and doubles as the idempotency guard for API-Q4.

findings.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
findings.description: No rate limiting exists at any layer present in the repository. The SOAP endpoint is published directly on the application server (soap:address http://partner-svc.acme-corp.internal:8080/po/PurchaseOrderService) with no API gateway, no WAF, and no throttling filter or interceptor in the source. Each call also opens its own Oracle connection via DriverManager with no pooling or connection cap, so a runaway agent loop would exhaust database connections as well as request threads.
findings.gap: A looping agent can saturate both the JBoss request threads and the Oracle 11g connection limit, taking the partner integration down for all partners. There is no enforced ceiling on call rate.
findings.recommendation: Place the endpoint behind a gateway with per-partner throttling, and at minimum introduce a pooled, capped datasource so per-call connection creation cannot exhaust the database.

findings.title: Blast Radius and Transaction Limits
findings.description: No business-domain limits exist. submitOrder accepts any amount parsed from the submitted XML and inserts it with no ceiling, no per-caller daily or hourly cap on order count or value, and no bulk-operation size limit. There is no per-identity configuration of any kind in the repository (no properties file, no IaC, no feature flags).
findings.gap: The blast radius of an agent error is unbounded in business terms: an agent loop could book an arbitrary number of orders at arbitrary values, and nothing in the system would stop or flag it.
findings.recommendation: Add per-partner business limits (max orders per hour, max order value, max cumulative value per session) enforced in the service and configurable per caller identity, independently of request-rate throttling.

findings.title: Draft/Pending State
findings.description: There is no intermediate state. The INSERT INTO partner_orders (partner_id, po_number, amount) statement writes the final record directly and the method immediately returns "ACCEPTED:" + poNumber - there is no status column in the inserted columns, no PENDING/DRAFT value, and no second confirm step in the WSDL (which declares only submitOrder).
findings.gap: An agent cannot propose an order for human review; every agent write is immediately committed as accepted, with no reviewable intermediate state and (per STATE-Q1) no way to reverse it.
findings.recommendation: Add a status column with a PENDING_REVIEW state and a separate confirm operation, so agent submissions can be staged and released by a human.

findings.title: Configurable Approval Gates
findings.description: No approval mechanism exists. The WSDL exposes a single fire-and-forget operation, and PurchaseOrderService.java contains no approval endpoint, no confirmation step, no operation-level flags, and no workflow state machine. Nothing can be configured to require human sign-off before the insert executes.
findings.gap: High-value or unusual agent submissions cannot be routed through human approval at the application layer; the service has no concept of an operation requiring confirmation.
findings.recommendation: Introduce per-operation, per-caller approval configuration (for example: orders above a configurable amount require explicit confirmation) enforced inside the service as defence in depth.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Classification
findings.description: Stage A = Yes: the system persists partner business and financial records (partner_orders with partner_id, po_number, amount) and handles partner credentials (README.md: 'Partner credentials stored in a flat properties file'; WS-Security PasswordText in plaintext), so it is a data-handling target in a financial/partner-identity domain. Stage B: B1 is clear - the only response is "ACCEPTED:<poNumber>" or an error string, so no sensitive stored field is serialized back to callers. B2 fires - all access runs through the single shared Oracle account partner_app with no scope, role, or column/row-level differentiation, so one credential grants everything the service can reach. B3 is absent - no classification tags, no field-level sensitivity annotations, and no PII-detection tooling anywhere in the repository.
findings.gap: No access-control differentiation between sensitive and non-sensitive data (B2): a caller either reaches the shared database account's full surface or nothing. Formal classification metadata is also absent (B3, informational).
findings.recommendation: Introduce scoped access for agent callers (distinct permission for order submission versus any future read of order history or partner details) and restrict the partner_app database grant to exactly the partner_orders insert it needs.

findings.title: Data Residency and Sovereignty
findings.description: No residency position is established. The data store is an on-premises Oracle 11g instance addressed by private IP (jdbc:oracle:thin:@10.0.9.30:1521:PARTDB) and README.md documents the deployment as JBoss AS 5.1 on RHEL 6 with no region, jurisdiction, or compliance statement. Searched README.md and all repository files for GDPR/LGPD/HIPAA/residency/sovereignty references and for any region or cross-region replication configuration: none exist. The data itself is partner identity plus commercial order values - a category commonly in scope for contractual and regulatory transfer restrictions.
findings.gap: Whether partner order data may leave the current jurisdiction - and therefore whether an agent may transmit it to an LLM endpoint in another region - is undetermined. There is no classification, no documented constraint, and no technical control preventing egress.
findings.recommendation: Determine and document the residency and sovereignty constraints on partner_orders and the partner credential store, then pin agent and LLM inference endpoints to a compliant region before any agent handles this data.

findings.title: PII Redaction in Logs
findings.description: The service has no logging framework at all, but it does propagate raw internal detail to callers: the catch block returns "ERROR:" + e.getMessage(), and the preceding SQL string embeds partnerId, poNumber and amount, so a SQLException message can echo the full statement - partner identifiers and order values - back over the wire. The JDBC URL and user are likewise exposed in connection-failure messages. No scrubbing, masking, or redaction utility exists (searched for log filters, masking libraries, and any logging configuration: none present); whatever JBoss writes to its own server log is unredacted by default.
findings.gap: Partner business data and infrastructure detail can leak into error responses and into container logs with no redaction layer. The surface-flag INFO downgrade does not apply because the system holds user/partner data (has_persistent_data_store = true).
findings.recommendation: Stop returning exception text to callers (return a correlation id instead), and add structured logging with explicit allowlisted fields plus masking for partner identifiers and order values.

findings.title: Documented API Interface
findings.description: The system exposes no REST, GraphQL, gRPC or AsyncAPI interface. The only integration surfaces are (a) direct VSAM/DB2 dataset access (`SELECT EMP-FILE ASSIGN TO EMPMAST`, `src/PAYRUN.cbl` lines 13-17) and (b) nightly plain-FTP transfer of a fixed-width flat file to an EC2 gateway (`jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` lines 14-21). README confirms: 'Integration: Nightly FTP of fixed-width files to/from EC2 gateway'. Searched for Express/Flask/Spring/gin route patterns, OpenAPI/Swagger/GraphQL/Smithy files and RPA scripts across all 4 repository files — zero results.
