findings.gap: No callable, documented programmatic interface exists for an agent to bind a tool to. Integration today requires dataset-level access or file drops, which are non-auditable, batch-latency-bound, and brittle.
findings.recommendation: Expose payroll read and calculation operations through an API facade (z/OS Connect EE, or an API Gateway + Lambda service in front of the EC2 gateway) with an OpenAPI contract, before attempting any agent integration.

findings.title: Idempotent Write Operations
findings.description: No idempotency mechanism exists. `PROCESS-EMP` (`src/PAYRUN.cbl` lines 44-56) unconditionally recomputes and `WRITE`s a pay record per employee, and the JCL allocates a new GDG generation each execution (`PAYOUT DD DSN=ACME.PAYROLL.PAYOUT(+1),DISP=(NEW,CATLG,DELETE)`). There is no run key, no idempotency token, no duplicate-run detection, and `STEP020` re-FTPs `ACME.PAYROLL.PAYOUT` unconditionally.
findings.gap: A retried or duplicated invocation produces a second payout file and a second plaintext FTP push, with no business key preventing duplicate payment for the same pay period.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a pay-period run key (period id + sequence) persisted and checked before processing, and make the FTP/publish step conditional on that key so re-execution is a no-op rather than a duplicate payout.

findings.title: Machine Identity Authentication
findings.description: No machine identity mechanism of any kind. The only authentication artifact in the repository is a shared static FTP userid and password embedded in JCL: `payroll PayR0ll2003!` (`jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` line 18). Job identity is the submitting human user (`NOTIFY=&SYSUID`). Searched for OAuth2 client-credentials, mTLS, API keys with principal attribution, Cognito app clients and API Gateway authorizers — none present.
findings.gap: There is no way to issue a distinct machine/agent principal, and no principal attribution available to downstream authorization or audit. Every invocation looks like the same shared `payroll` account or the submitting RACF user.
findings.recommendation: Provision a distinct machine identity per agent (IAM role or OAuth2 client-credentials client at the API facade, RACF/ACF2 surrogate id on the mainframe side) and carry the principal through to DB2/dataset access.

findings.title: Scoped Permissions (Least Privilege)
findings.description: Authorization is entirely coarse-grained. The job runs with `REGION=0M` (unbounded storage) under the submitter's identity, datasets are shared with `DISP=SHR` (`jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` lines 1-7), and the one credential present (`payroll`) is a single shared account used for the whole transfer. No IAM policies, RACF profile definitions, scopes, or any other mechanism for differentiating access levels exist in the repository.
findings.gap: There is no mechanism to grant a caller read-only access to a subset of payroll data. Any identity that can run or read this job inherits the full surface.
findings.recommendation: Define scoped profiles per capability (read-employee-summary vs. generate-payout vs. transmit) as RACF dataset profiles and, at the future API facade, IAM/OAuth scopes bound to the machine identity.

findings.title: Action-Level Authorization
findings.description: No action-level authorization. There are no permission checks in `src/PAYRUN.cbl` — the program unconditionally opens `EMP-FILE` for input and `PAY-FILE` for output (lines 37-38) with authority derived solely from the batch job's identity. No `canRead`/`canWrite` equivalents, ABAC policies, or method-level authorization exist anywhere (no middleware, no IaC, no API layer).
findings.gap: Read and write authority are inseparable: anything permitted to invoke the payroll calculation is permitted to generate and transmit a payout. An agent restricted to reads cannot be enforced technically.
findings.recommendation: Split the read path from the write path into separately authorized operations at the API facade and bind distinct RACF/IAM permissions to each, so read-only agent scope is enforceable rather than declarative.

findings.title: Identity Propagation and Delegation
findings.description: No identity propagation or delegation. The only identity in the pipeline is `NOTIFY=&SYSUID` (the submitting user, `jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` line 1) for notification purposes and the shared `payroll` FTP account for the transfer hop (line 18). No JWT parsing, token exchange, on-behalf-of flow, or user-context header exists, and the COBOL program receives no caller context at all.
findings.gap: The system cannot distinguish an agent acting as itself from an agent acting on behalf of a specific user, and no caller identity survives the FTP hop to the EC2 gateway — the gateway sees only the shared account.
findings.recommendation: Carry a propagated principal (and, where applicable, an on-behalf-of subject) from the API facade through to the batch invocation and the gateway hop, and record both actor and subject distinctly.

findings.title: Credential Management
findings.description: A production credential is hardcoded in version-controlled source: `payroll PayR0ll2003!` in the inline FTP input of `STEP020` (`jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` line 18). The JCL comment states 'DATASET NAMES AND DB2 CREDS HARDCODED - SEE OPS RUNBOOK' (line 4) and README lists 'Hardcoded dataset names and credentials in JCL' as a known issue. No Secrets Manager, Vault, or any secrets-management reference exists; the password's embedded year suggests it has not rotated since 2003.
findings.gap: A long-lived plaintext credential for the payroll transfer account is readable by anyone with repository access and is present in git history. No rotation mechanism exists.
findings.recommendation: Rotate the `payroll` account credential immediately, move it to AWS Secrets Manager (or the mainframe equivalent) with scheduled rotation, and retrieve it at run time rather than embedding it in JCL. Treat the current value as compromised and purge it from history.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: No audit logging of the authenticated principal for write operations. The program emits only `SYSOUT DD SYSOUT=*` (`jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` line 13) — unstructured spool output with no principal field. There is no CloudTrail, no S3 Object Lock, no log retention or tamper-evidence configuration anywhere in the repository (no IaC files exist at all).
findings.gap: Payroll disbursement writes (PAYOUT generation and FTP push) produce no immutable, attributable audit record. Agent-initiated actions could not be distinguished from human-initiated runs, nor proven for SOX purposes.
findings.recommendation: Emit a structured per-run audit record (principal, run key, record count, totals, timestamp) to an append-only store (SMF offload or S3 with Object Lock) and attribute it to the machine identity from AUTH-Q1.

findings.title: Agent Identity Suspension
findings.description: No per-identity suspension or revocation capability. There is a single shared FTP account (`jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` line 18) and no API keys, service accounts, IAM roles, or user-pool entries that could be individually disabled. Revoking access would mean disabling the one shared `payroll` account, which stops the entire payroll pipeline.
findings.gap: A misbehaving agent identity cannot be isolated without taking down payroll processing for everyone — there is no per-identity kill switch.
findings.recommendation: Issue one revocable credential/role per consuming identity and verify that disabling an individual identity leaves the batch pipeline and other consumers operational.

findings.title: Compensation and Rollback
findings.description: No compensation or rollback. `MAIN-PARA` (`src/PAYRUN.cbl` lines 36-43) opens the files, loops to EOF and `STOP RUN`s; there is no file-status checking, no checkpoint/restart, no undo of records already written, and no coordination between `STEP010` (compute/write) and `STEP020` (FTP push) in `jcl/PAYRUN.jcl`. An abend after partial processing leaves a partial PAYOUT generation catalogued, and a failure after FTP leaves the gateway holding a partial file.
findings.gap: The two-step write sequence (compute+write, then transmit) has no compensating action. Partial state is neither detected nor reversible.
findings.recommendation: Add checkpoint/restart (or a staging dataset promoted only on clean completion), explicit FILE STATUS handling in the COBOL, and make STEP020 conditional (`COND`/`IF`) on STEP010 completion so a failed run cannot publish partial payroll.

findings.title: Concurrency Controls
findings.description: No concurrency control. `EMP-FILE` is opened `ACCESS MODE IS SEQUENTIAL` with `DISP=SHR` on `ACME.PAYROLL.EMPMAST` (`src/PAYRUN.cbl` lines 13-17, `jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` line 7) — shared disposition with no enqueue, no record-level locking, no version field in `EMP-RECORD`, and no optimistic-concurrency token. Nothing prevents two concurrent PAYRUN executions, and both would write to their own new GDG generation from the same mutable master.
findings.gap: Concurrent invocations can read the employee master mid-update and produce divergent or duplicated payout files; there is no conflict detection to reject the second writer.
findings.recommendation: Add a run-level enqueue (dataset ENQ or a scheduler mutex) so only one payroll calculation can execute per period, and add a version/last-updated column to the employee master for optimistic concurrency at the record level.

findings.title: Circuit Breakers and Resilience
findings.description: No resilience controls on external dependencies. `READ-EMP` (`src/PAYRUN.cbl` lines 57-59) handles only `AT END` — there is no `FILE STATUS` clause, no I/O error branch, and no `INVALID KEY` handling. The FTP step (`jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` lines 15-21) runs a fixed inline script with no timeout, no retry, no return-code check and no failure path if `10.0.7.40` is unreachable. README notes DB2 v10 is out of support and the batch window overruns at 5-7 hours.
findings.gap: A slow or unavailable dependency (DB2, the EC2 gateway) produces an abend or a silent partial result rather than a bounded, retried, circuit-broken failure — and an agent calling in would observe no distinction.
findings.recommendation: Add FILE STATUS and I/O error handling to the COBOL, bounded retries with backoff and a return-code gate on the transfer step, and a timeout/circuit-breaker at the API facade that fails fast instead of queueing behind a 5-7 hour batch.

findings.title: Blast Radius and Transaction Limits
findings.description: No blast-radius or transaction limits. `PERFORM PROCESS-EMP UNTIL WS-EOF = 'Y'` (`src/PAYRUN.cbl` line 41) processes the entire employee master unconditionally — there is no maximum-records cap, no total-disbursement ceiling, no per-caller batch-size limit, and no spend threshold. `SPACE=(CYL,(50,10),RLSE)` is a storage allocation, not a business limit.
findings.gap: A single invocation can generate payout records for every employee with no cap on record count or total monetary value, so an erroneous agent-initiated run has unbounded financial blast radius.
findings.recommendation: Add configurable per-run business limits (max employees processed, max aggregate net disbursement, max variance vs. prior period) that abort the run and require explicit human override when exceeded.

findings.title: Draft/Pending State
findings.description: No draft or pending state. `PROCESS-EMP` writes final pay records directly (`WRITE PAY-RECORD`, `src/PAYRUN.cbl` line 55) and the output generation is immediately catalogued (`DISP=(NEW,CATLG,DELETE)`) and FTP'd to the gateway in the next step. `PAY-RECORD` is an opaque `PIC X(120)` with no status field, and there is no PENDING/DRAFT/PROPOSED state or create-then-confirm sequence anywhere.
findings.gap: There is no reviewable intermediate state between calculation and disbursement, so a proposed payroll run cannot be inspected and approved before it is committed and transmitted.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a proposed-run state: write to a staging dataset with an explicit status, and promote/transmit only on an approval action. This also provides the review point HITL-Q2 needs.

findings.title: Configurable Approval Gates
findings.description: No configurable approval gate. The pipeline is a fully automated CA-7 schedule — `jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` line 3 states 'RUNS EVERY OTHER FRIDAY VIA CA-7 SCHEDULE PAYRUN-BW' and `STEP020` transmits immediately after `STEP010` with no intervening confirmation step, approval endpoint, or operation-level flag. No approval API, no waitForTaskToken-equivalent, no manual hold is defined.
findings.gap: High-impact operations (generating and transmitting a payroll disbursement file) cannot be configured to require human approval at the system layer; the only control is the scheduler.
findings.recommendation: Add an operation-level approval flag that holds the transmit step pending explicit human release, configurable per operation type (e.g., always required for off-cycle runs or runs exceeding the STATE-Q6 limits).

findings.title: Sensitive Data Classification
findings.description: Stage A = Yes: the employee master record holds `EMP-SSN PIC 9(09)` and `EMP-ACCT PIC X(17)` (bank account) alongside name, rate and hours (`src/PAYRUN.cbl` lines 21-27), and README lists 'Plaintext FTP of SSN and bank account data' as a known issue. Stage B1 fires: there is no field scoping of any kind — `STEP020` transmits the whole `ACME.PAYROLL.PAYOUT` dataset over plain FTP, and any consumer reading `EMPMAST` receives the full record including SSN and account number. Stage B2 fires: access is dataset-level with `DISP=SHR` and a single shared `payroll` credential — no differentiation between sensitive and non-sensitive access. Stage B3: no classification tags, field annotations, or Macie-equivalent tooling exist.
findings.gap: Sensitive fields (SSN, bank account) are not excluded from, or separately authorized within, the data a consumer or agent would retrieve. One credential grants everything.
findings.recommendation: Define a scoped projection for agent consumption that omits SSN and account number (separate, separately-authorized endpoint for the disbursement path only), and add field-level classification annotations to the record layout and its API representation.

findings.title: Data Residency and Sovereignty
findings.description: Payroll data containing SSN and bank account numbers is transmitted unencrypted across a trust boundary to an EC2-hosted gateway at a hardcoded private IP (`open 10.0.7.40`, `ascii`, `put 'ACME.PAYROLL.PAYOUT' /incoming/payout.dat`, `jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` lines 14-21). No residency, sovereignty, region-pinning or cross-region replication control appears anywhere in the repository, and no GDPR/LGPD/jurisdictional statement exists in `README.md` — the only compliance-adjacent note is that the plaintext FTP of SSN and bank data is a known issue.
findings.gap: There is no declared or enforced boundary for where this regulated payroll data may travel, and no encryption in transit on the one hop that does cross a boundary. Nothing would prevent an agent from relaying the data to an out-of-jurisdiction endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Classify the payroll dataset's residency constraints explicitly, replace plain FTP with an encrypted, region-pinned transfer (SFTP/TLS to an in-region endpoint), and record the permitted-destination policy as enforceable configuration.

findings.title: PII Redaction in Logs
findings.description: No PII redaction in observable output. The job writes diagnostics to `SYSOUT DD SYSOUT=*` (`jcl/PAYRUN.jcl` line 13) — unfiltered JES spool with no scrubbing layer. The processed records contain `EMP-SSN` and `EMP-ACCT` (`src/PAYRUN.cbl` lines 25-26), and any abend dump or diagnostic trace of the record area would expose them verbatim. No log-scrubbing middleware, masking utility, CloudWatch filter, or Macie-equivalent exists in the repository.
findings.gap: Employee SSNs and bank account numbers sit in the working record area with no masking policy, so abend dumps and spool output are an uncontrolled PII egress path.
findings.recommendation: Mask SSN and account fields in any diagnostic output, route spool to a retention-bounded, access-controlled destination, and add a redaction filter before logs reach any downstream observability system.

findings.title: No documented machine-consumable API interface
findings.description:
The only integration surface is a single Apache CGI endpoint, /cgi-bin/pricing.cgi?sku=&qty=, implemented in pricing.cpp. main() reads the QUERY_STRING environment variable and emits an HTML document with printf (Content-Type: text/html). There are no REST resources, no GraphQL schema, no AsyncAPI definition, and no JSON representation. Consuming this service from an agent tool requires scraping

Unit: $...

out of an HTML page. No OpenAPI/Swagger, GraphQL, Smithy, or AsyncAPI file exists anywhere in the repository (searched for openapi.*, swagger.*, *.graphql, *.gql, *.smithy, and framework route declarations; the repository contains only pricing.cpp, Makefile, Dockerfile, k8s/*.yaml, and markdown).
findings.gap: No documented, structured API contract. Integration is HTML-screen-scraping against a presentation-formatted response, which is the brittle coupling API-Q1 is designed to detect.
findings.recommendation: Front the pricing calculation with a documented JSON interface: add a thin HTTP service (or an API Gateway + Lambda/sidecar wrapper) exposing GET /v1/prices?sku=&qty= returning {"sku","quantity","unit_price","total_price","currency","as_of"}, and publish an OpenAPI description of it. Keep the CGI path only for legacy callers.

findings.title: No machine identity authentication on the CGI surface
findings.description: The service performs no authentication of any kind. pricing.cpp reads QUERY_STRING and responds unconditionally; there is no token parsing, API key check, or principal lookup. The Dockerfile configures Apache with 'Require all granted' on /usr/local/apache2/cgi-bin, so every request to port 8080 is served anonymously. k8s/service.yaml is a ClusterIP Service with no authorizer, and the commented ALB Ingress example in the same file adds no authentication annotations. No OAuth2 client-credentials flow, mTLS configuration, service account, Cognito app client, or API Gateway authorizer exists (searched all of pricing.cpp, Dockerfile, and k8s/*.yaml; no IaC or identity provider configuration is present in the repository).
findings.gap: There is no mechanism to identify a calling principal, so no agent call can be attributed, scoped, rate-limited per identity, or revoked. Every downstream authorization and audit control is unimplementable without this.
findings.recommendation: Terminate agent traffic at an authenticating layer before the CGI binary: an ALB/API Gateway with an OIDC or IAM authorizer, or a mesh sidecar enforcing mTLS, passing a verified principal identifier to the backend. Issue a distinct machine identity per agent so calls are attributable.

findings.title: No authorization model, therefore no scoped permissions
findings.description: No authorization model exists at any layer. pricing.cpp contains no permission check between parsing the query string and returning a price. The Apache configuration generated in the Dockerfile grants 'Require all granted' to the cgi-bin directory. There are no IAM policies, API Gateway resource policies, or RBAC definitions in the repository — k8s/ contains only namespace, configmap, deployment, and service manifests with no Role, RoleBinding, or NetworkPolicy. Because all callers receive identical access, there is no mechanism to grant one agent identity narrower access than another.
findings.gap: No capability to differentiate access levels per caller. An agent identity cannot be constrained to a subset of SKUs, endpoints, or operations; it inherits the full surface by default.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a scoped authorization layer at the ingress — e.g., API Gateway with per-client usage identity plus scope claims, or an IAM policy per agent role restricted to the pricing route — so each agent credential carries only the access its task requires.

findings.title: No action-level authorization enforcement point
findings.description: The binary exposes a single implicit read action and enforces nothing. There are no canRead/canWrite/canDelete style checks, no ABAC or RBAC permission matrix, and no method-level authorization configuration. Apache's generated configuration (Dockerfile) sets Options +ExecCGI with 'Require all granted' and does not constrain HTTP methods, so the CGI binary is invoked for any method reaching the path; pricing.cpp ignores REQUEST_METHOD entirely and always executes the same code path.
findings.gap: No mechanism exists to permit some operations and deny others per caller. If the service later gains write or administrative paths, there is no enforcement point to attach action-level rules to, and today no method restriction exists at all.
findings.recommendation: Add an authorization enforcement point at the ingress or in a wrapper service that is keyed on operation (and, at minimum, restrict the CGI route to GET via Apache <LimitExcept> or gateway method configuration).

findings.title: No rate limiting or throttling on the agent-callable endpoint
findings.description: No rate limiting exists at any layer. pricing.cpp has no request accounting. The Apache configuration assembled in the Dockerfile enables cgid/cgi modules and the cgi-bin ScriptAlias but sets no mod_ratelimit, mod_qos, or MaxRequestWorkers tuning. k8s/service.yaml is a plain ClusterIP Service and the Ingress example in its comments carries only ALB scheme/target-type annotations — no WAF rate rule, no API Gateway usage plan (no IaC of any kind exists in the repository). The only bound is the per-pod CPU limit of 500m across 2 replicas in k8s/deployment.yaml, which is a saturation point, not a throttle. Because every request forks a CGI process and re-opens and re-scans /etc/pricing/rules.dat (lookup_price, pricing.cpp), machine-speed calling is unusually expensive per request.
findings.gap: A runaway agent loop can saturate the deployment at machine speed with no per-caller ceiling and no 429 response; failure mode is pod CPU exhaustion and probe failure rather than graceful rejection.
findings.recommendation: Enforce request-rate limits in front of the service — AWS WAF rate-based rules or an API Gateway usage plan on the agent-facing route — and return 429 with Retry-After so callers can self-throttle.

findings.title: Documented API Interface
findings.description: The only callable surface is a Rails 2.3 HTML controller. `OrdersController` (app/controllers/orders_controller.rb) exposes `index`, `create` and `show` actions that terminate in `render :action` and `redirect_to` — server-rendered views, not a content-negotiated API. There is no `respond_to`/`respond_with` block, no `format.json`, no `/api` namespace, no GraphQL schema (`.graphql`/`.gql`), no AsyncAPI or Smithy model, and no routes file in the repository. Searched: file names matching `openapi.*`, `swagger.*`, `*.graphql`, `*.gql`, `*.smithy`, `*.proto`; the full file inventory (4 files); README architecture section.
findings.gap: No machine-callable interface exists. An agent could only integrate by driving the HTML UI (RPA) or by connecting directly to MySQL 5.1 — both brittle, unauditable couplings. Agent tool binding has no stable contract to bind to.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a JSON API surface in front of the order domain — either a versioned `/api/v1/orders` controller with `respond_to :json` on a supported Rails release, or a thin API facade service that fronts the legacy app. Publish it as an OpenAPI document and make that the only integration path for agents.

findings.title: Idempotent Write Operations
findings.description: `OrdersController#create` accepts `params[:order]`, saves a new `Order`, and then calls `charge_card(@order)`, which invokes `gateway.charge(order.total, order.card_number, order.card_exp)` against a live payment gateway (`mode: live` in config/payment.yml). There is no idempotency key parameter, no idempotency middleware, no lookup of an existing order by a business key, and no unique constraint visible in the repository. Each repeated POST creates a new order row and issues a new charge.
findings.gap: No idempotency protection on a money-moving write endpoint. An agent retry — or a duplicated LLM tool call — double-charges the customer's card and creates duplicate orders.
findings.recommendation: Require a caller-supplied `Idempotency-Key` on order creation, persist it with a unique index, and return the original order (and its original charge result) on replay. Pass the same key through to the payment gateway so the downstream charge is also deduplicated.

findings.title: Machine Identity Authentication
findings.description: No authentication mechanism exists in the repository. `OrdersController` carries the comment `# No before_filter auth on some actions (legacy oversight)` and declares no `before_filter`/`before_action` at all. There is no OAuth2 client-credentials flow, no API key validation with principal attribution, no mTLS configuration, no service-account definition, no Cognito/IdP integration, and no API Gateway authorizer. README states sessions are cookie-stored with the secret in source control, which is a human-browser session mechanism, not machine identity.
findings.gap: The system cannot authenticate a non-human caller or attribute a request to a specific agent principal. Every downstream authorization and audit decision (AUTH-Q2, AUTH-Q3, AUTH-Q6) is therefore unenforceable.
findings.recommendation: Front the order API with an authenticating edge (API Gateway authorizer or OAuth2 client-credentials via an IdP), issue a distinct machine identity per agent, and propagate the resolved principal into the application request context so it can be logged and authorized.

findings.title: Scoped Permissions (Least Privilege)
findings.description: There is no authorization model to scope. The controller performs no permission checks before `Order.find_by_sql`, `Order.new`, or `Order.find`. No IAM policies, API Gateway resource policies, role definitions, or permission constants exist in the repository (no IaC files were found).
findings.gap: All authorization is effectively absent, which is the extreme case of coarse-grained: there is no mechanism to grant an agent read-only access to orders without also granting order creation and card charging. Blast radius cannot be scoped down.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a scope/role model for the order domain (e.g. `orders:read`, `orders:create`, `payments:charge`) enforced at the edge and re-checked in the controller, and bind each agent identity to the minimum scope set it needs.

findings.title: Action-Level Authorization
findings.description: No action-level authorization is enforced. `index` (read), `create` (write plus payment charge) and `show` (read) are all reachable with identical (absent) authorization. There are no `canRead`/`canWrite`-style checks, no ABAC policy, no permission matrix, and no method-level gateway authorization.
findings.gap: An agent granted access in order to read order history is simultaneously able to create orders and charge cards, because read and write actions share the same (nonexistent) gate.
findings.recommendation: Enforce per-action authorization in a `before_filter` keyed on the authenticated principal's scopes, so a read-scoped agent identity is rejected on `create`.

findings.title: Identity Propagation and Delegation
findings.description: No identity propagation exists. The controller reads no `Authorization`, `X-User-Id`, or equivalent caller-context header, performs no JWT parsing, and uses no token-exchange or on-behalf-of flow. The outbound call to the payment gateway authenticates with a static shared merchant credential (`PaymentGateway.new(cfg['merchant_id'], cfg['api_password'])`) with no caller context attached. README describes cookie sessions as the only identity mechanism.
findings.gap: The system cannot distinguish an agent acting under its own service identity from an agent acting on behalf of a specific customer, and cannot bound the latter by that customer's permissions — a privilege-escalation path for any on-behalf-of agent workflow.
findings.recommendation: Adopt token-based identity with distinct claims for actor (agent) and subject (user), validate both at the API boundary, and record both on every order mutation. Keep separate credentials for agent-as-self versus user-delegated calls.

findings.title: Credential Management
findings.description: Live payment-gateway credentials are committed to source control. `config/payment.yml` contains `merchant_id: ACME-MERCH-0042`, `api_password: payGw2008secret`, `endpoint: https://gateway.legacy-pay.example.com/soap/v1` and `mode: live`, and the file's own header comment acknowledges this. `OrdersController#charge_card` loads it at request time via `YAML.load_file("#{RAILS_ROOT}/config/payment.yml")`. No `aws_secretsmanager_*` resources, Vault client, or rotation mechanism exist; README separately notes the session secret is also in source control. `.gitignore` excludes `.env` files but not `config/payment.yml`.
findings.gap: Production payment credentials are readable by anyone with repository access and persist in git history, with no rotation path. An agent bug or prompt-injection that can read application config or echo file contents can exfiltrate a live merchant credential.
findings.recommendation: Move the merchant credential to AWS Secrets Manager (or Vault) with automatic rotation, load it at boot from the secret store, purge `config/payment.yml` from the working tree and rewrite/rotate the exposed credential as compromised. Treat the cookie session secret the same way.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: No audit logging of write operations exists. `create` saves an order and charges a card without writing any audit record, and no authenticated principal is available to log (AUTH-Q1). There is no `aws_cloudtrail` resource, no log-file validation, no S3 Object Lock bucket, and no log-retention configuration — the repository contains no IaC. `.gitignore` ignores `*.log`, and README documents no log pipeline; application logs are local Mongrel/Rails files on EC2 hosts and are mutable.
findings.gap: Card charges and order mutations are not attributable or tamper-evident. Agent-initiated financial writes could not be reconstructed or proven in a forensic or compliance review (PCI/SOX-relevant given live card handling).
findings.recommendation: Emit a structured audit event for every order mutation and charge — principal, actor/subject, operation, target id, outcome, timestamp — to an append-only sink (CloudWatch Logs with retention plus S3 with Object Lock, or CloudTrail for the data plane), and enable log-file validation.

findings.title: Agent Identity Suspension
findings.description: There is no agent identity to suspend. No API key store or revocation endpoint, no IAM role or service-account disable path, and no IdP integration exist in the repository. The only identity mechanism README describes is a cookie session signed with a secret held in source control — revoking it would require rotating that shared secret and invalidating every session, i.e. a platform-wide outage.
findings.gap: A misbehaving agent cannot be isolated. The only available kill switch is taking down the storefront for all callers, human and machine.
findings.recommendation: Issue per-agent credentials from a revocable store (API Gateway keys, IdP client credentials, or IAM roles) so a single agent identity can be disabled immediately without affecting other callers.

findings.title: Compensation and Rollback
findings.description: `OrdersController#create` performs a two-step write with no compensation: `@order.save` persists the order, then `charge_card(@order)` calls the gateway. `charge_card` has no `rescue`, no transaction wrapper, and no reversal path — if the SOAP charge fails or times out, the saved order remains while no payment was captured; if the charge succeeds but the subsequent `redirect_to`/persistence path fails, the charge is not recorded against a confirmed order. There are no compensating-transaction, saga, undo-endpoint, or two-phase-commit patterns anywhere in the repository.
findings.gap: Multi-step writes can be left in a partial state with no rollback or compensation, and there is no undo endpoint an agent (or operator) could call to reverse an order or refund a charge.
findings.recommendation: Wrap order creation and charge capture in an explicit state machine (`pending` → `authorized` → `captured` → `failed`) with a compensating refund/void action on failure, and expose a reversal operation. Authorize first, capture only after the order is durably committed.

findings.title: Concurrency Controls
findings.description: No concurrency control is present. `Order.new(params[:order])` / `@order.save` performs an unconditional insert; `Order.find(params[:id])` in `show` reads without version checks; `index` issues a raw `find_by_sql` with no locking clause. There is no `lock_version` column reference (Rails optimistic locking), no `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, no ETag/`If-Match` handling, and no conflict-resolution logic in the repository.
findings.gap: Concurrent agent instances creating or updating orders can interleave without detection, producing duplicate orders and lost updates — compounded by the absence of idempotency keys (API-Q4).
findings.recommendation: Add Rails optimistic locking (`lock_version`) to mutable order records, return/require ETags on the API, and reject conflicting writes with a distinguishable 409 so agents can re-read and retry safely.

findings.title: Circuit Breakers and Resilience
findings.description: The outbound dependency call has no resilience controls. `charge_card` constructs `PaymentGateway.new(...)` and calls `gateway.charge(...)` with no timeout, no retry policy, no exponential backoff, and no circuit breaker; the target is a deprecated SOAP endpoint (`config/payment.yml` `endpoint`), which README confirms is a direct integration with a deprecated gateway SOAP API. No resilience library is declared (no dependency manifest exists).
findings.gap: A slow or failing payment gateway blocks Mongrel worker threads indefinitely and cascades back to the caller. A looping agent would exhaust the worker pool and take the storefront down with it.
findings.recommendation: Set explicit connect/read timeouts on the gateway client, add bounded retries with backoff only for idempotent/authorized operations, and wrap the call in a circuit breaker that fails fast with a retryable error signal when the gateway is unhealthy.

findings.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
findings.description: No rate limiting exists at any layer. There is no API Gateway or WAF in the architecture — README describes Mongrel behind Apache `mod_proxy_balancer` on a fixed set of EC2 hosts — and no `aws_api_gateway_usage_plan` or equivalent IaC exists. No application-level throttling middleware is present; the controller applies no per-caller limits. Searched the full file inventory and README architecture/deployment sections.
findings.gap: A runaway agent loop can saturate the Mongrel cluster at machine speed, and every request to `create` also issues a live gateway charge. There is no protective ceiling in front of production.
findings.recommendation: Terminate agent traffic at an API Gateway (or Apache/WAF rate rules) with a per-API-key request budget, and add application-level throttling on `create` as defence in depth.

findings.title: Blast Radius and Transaction Limits
findings.description: No business-domain transaction limits exist. `create` charges `order.total` with no per-caller spend cap, no maximum charges per hour, and no bulk-operation size limit; `index` returns every matching order with no cap. Searched the controller and `config/payment.yml` for limit/threshold configuration — `payment.yml` contains only `merchant_id`, `api_password`, `endpoint` and `mode`.
findings.gap: There is no ceiling on the business impact of a correct-but-catastrophic agent loop. An agent repeatedly invoking `create` can issue unlimited live charges; nothing bounds spend per session or records touched per run.
findings.recommendation: Introduce configurable per-identity business limits — maximum charge amount per order, maximum cumulative spend per hour per agent identity, maximum records per bulk read/write — enforced server-side and independent of request-rate throttling.

findings.title: Configurable Approval Gates
findings.description: No approval gate mechanism exists. `create` saves and charges in a single uninterrupted request path with no confirmation step; there are no approval endpoints, no per-operation configuration flags, and no workflow engine (no Step Functions or `waitForTaskToken` usage — the repository contains no IaC). The `status` field is read in `index` but never used to gate the charge in `create`.
findings.gap: High-risk operations — order creation with a live card charge — cannot be configured to require human approval, so there is no application-layer defence in depth for an agent-initiated payment.
findings.recommendation: Add an operation-level approval configuration: when enabled for `charge`, persist the order as `pending_approval`, require an explicit approve call from an authorized human principal before capture, and record the approver in the audit trail.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Classification
findings.description: The system handles payment-card data and returns it unscoped. `index` executes `Order.find_by_sql("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = '#{status}' ...")` — an unprojected `SELECT *` over a table whose columns include `card_number` and `card_exp` (both read in `charge_card`) — and `show` returns `Order.find(params[:id])` whole. There is no `attr_accessible`/serializer exclusion (README: `attr_accessible` not used), no separate response DTO, no column projection, and no field-level filtering. There is also no access-control differentiation of any kind (AUTH-Q2/Q3), and no classification metadata: no field sensitivity annotations, no PII tooling (Macie/Presidio), no data catalog, and no IaC tags.
findings.gap: B1 fired: general-purpose read endpoints return full card numbers and expiry data to any caller, including an agent that has no business retrieving them. B2 fired: a single (absent) permission grants access to everything sensitive. B3: no formal classification metadata exists.
findings.recommendation: Project explicitly in agent-facing reads (`select` only non-sensitive columns), never return `card_number`/`card_exp` from list or detail endpoints, and replace stored card data with a gateway token. Then add scope separation (`orders:read` vs `payments:read`) and field-level sensitivity annotations.

findings.title: Data Residency and Sovereignty
findings.description: The system persists regulated payment data (card number and expiry in MySQL, per `charge_card` field access) and transmits it to an external SOAP gateway, but no residency or sovereignty controls are expressed anywhere. Searched README, `config/payment.yml`, and the full file inventory for GDPR/LGPD/PCI references, region pinning, cross-region replication settings, and data-sovereignty policy — none found. `config/payment.yml` records only an endpoint hostname (`gateway.legacy-pay.example.com`) with no stated jurisdiction; README states MySQL 5.1 runs on a separate EC2 instance without naming a region.
findings.gap: The jurisdiction of both the data store and the payment endpoint is undocumented, so there is no basis on which to decide whether order or card data may be sent to an LLM endpoint in another region. Absence of a documented constraint is not evidence that none applies.
findings.recommendation: Document the governing regimes for order and card data (PCI DSS plus any applicable GDPR/LGPD obligations), pin the data store and any agent/LLM endpoints to approved regions, and encode the allowed-region list in configuration that the integration layer enforces before any payload leaves the boundary.

findings.title: PII Redaction in Logs
findings.description: No PII or cardholder-data redaction exists. `charge_card` passes `order.card_number` and `order.card_exp` into `gateway.charge`, and the controller has no rescue block — a gateway exception in Rails 2.3 is logged with the backtrace and surrounding request context, and Rails request logging records parameters, so `params[:order]` card fields can reach the application log. No log-scrubbing middleware, PII-masking library, CloudWatch log filter, or Macie integration is present; `.gitignore` merely excludes `*.log` from the repository, which prevents commits, not leakage.
findings.gap: Full card numbers and customer details can land in plaintext application logs on the EC2 hosts, with no masking and (per AUTH-Q6) no controlled retention — a PCI exposure that widens as agents drive request volume.
findings.recommendation: Add a log parameter filter for card and personal fields (Rails `filter_parameter_logging`-equivalent), mask card numbers to last-four everywhere outside the gateway call, and never log request bodies for the order endpoints. Pair with structured logging (OBS-Q1) so the allowlist is explicit.

findings.title: Documented API Interface
findings.description: Only integration surface is the ASP.NET WebForms page Timesheet.aspx.vb, whose Page_Load and btnSave_Click postback handlers read and write SQL directly. No REST controller, GraphQL schema, AsyncAPI spec, or Smithy model exists in the repository.
findings.gap: Integration requires UI automation of ViewState postbacks or direct SQL Server access - brittle and non-auditable.
findings.recommendation: Extract the read and insert logic into a service layer and expose it as a versioned HTTP API.

findings.title: Idempotent Write Operations
findings.description: btnSave_Click issues an unconditional INSERT INTO timesheets with no idempotency key, no business-key uniqueness check, and no read-before-write.
findings.gap: No idempotency mechanism in the write path; a retried submit creates duplicate timesheet rows.
findings.recommendation: Add a unique constraint on (employee_id, entry_date, project) and accept a caller-supplied idempotency key.

findings.title: Machine Identity Authentication
findings.description: web.config configures only interactive Forms authentication (loginUrl=Login.aspx, requireSSL=false); the identity used by the data layer is Session("EmployeeId"). No OAuth2 client-credentials flow, API key with principal attribution, or mTLS exists.
findings.gap: No machine principal can authenticate and no non-human caller can be attributed.
findings.recommendation: Introduce an identity provider issuing service-principal tokens and accept bearer tokens at the API boundary.

findings.title: Scoped Permissions (Least Privilege)
findings.description: All callers authenticate through one Forms-auth flow, and the application connects to SQL Server as the single shared login ts_app. There are no roles, no <authorization> section, and no per-principal policy.
findings.gap: No mechanism exists to grant a read-only, resource-scoped identity.
findings.recommendation: Introduce role-based authorization and distinct database principals per access level.

findings.title: Action-Level Authorization
findings.description: Neither BindGrid() (read) nor btnSave_Click (write) performs a permission check; both execute for any authenticated session. No canRead/canWrite checks or method-level authorization exist.
findings.gap: Read access cannot be granted without implicitly granting write access.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit per-operation authorization checks before each data access call.

findings.title: Identity Propagation and Delegation
findings.description: Identity is carried as Session("EmployeeId") in an InProc session. No token is parsed, no Authorization header is handled, and there is no way to distinguish an acting principal from a data subject.
findings.gap: On-behalf-of flows are impossible; a caller would have to assume a human's session.
findings.recommendation: Adopt token-based identity with separate actor and subject claims.

findings.title: Credential Management
findings.description: The SQL Server password is hardcoded in plaintext in web.config (User ID=ts_app;Password=Time2006!). The configuration section is not encrypted, no secrets manager or Vault integration exists, and there is no rotation mechanism. debug=true and customErrors mode=Off widen exposure on error pages.
findings.gap: A static, shared, plaintext production credential committed to source control with no rotation.
findings.recommendation: Rotate the exposed password immediately and move the credential to a managed secrets store with scheduled rotation.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: The INSERT in btnSave_Click executes with no log record of the acting principal. web.config declares no trace, health-monitoring, or log sink, and customErrors mode=Off routes failures to the browser.
findings.gap: No audit trail at all, let alone an immutable, tamper-evident one.
findings.recommendation: Write append-only audit records (principal, operation, entity key) to immutable storage with retention policy.

findings.title: Agent Identity Suspension
findings.description: No API key store, role deactivation path, or per-principal disable mechanism exists. Revoking access means rotating the shared ts_app credential or taking the single IIS site offline.
findings.gap: One misbehaving caller cannot be isolated without affecting all users.
findings.recommendation: Issue per-principal credentials with an immediate revocation path.

findings.title: Compensation and Rollback
findings.description: btnSave_Click executes a single ExecuteNonQuery then rebinds the grid. There is no SqlTransaction, no TransactionScope, no undo endpoint, and no compensating transaction.
findings.gap: Failures after the insert leave the write committed with no rollback path; multi-step agent workflows cannot be unwound.
findings.recommendation: Wrap writes in an explicit transaction scope and expose a reversal (void/correct) operation.

findings.title: Concurrency Controls
findings.description: The INSERT uses no version column, no If-Match/ETag, no SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, and no conditional write. Session/ViewState is the only coordination mechanism.
findings.gap: Concurrent callers can create conflicting or duplicate entries for the same employee and date.
findings.recommendation: Add optimistic concurrency (row version) plus a unique business-key constraint.

findings.title: Circuit Breakers and Resilience
findings.description: SqlConnection and SqlCommand are used with default timeouts and no retry, backoff, or circuit breaker. No resilience library is declared (the repository contains no dependency manifest).
findings.gap: SQL Server slowness propagates directly to callers as hung requests.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit command timeouts and a retry/circuit-breaker policy around data access.

findings.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
findings.description: web.config declares no request-rate or handler limits, and no API gateway or WAF is defined anywhere in the repository. The app runs on a single IIS 6 host with InProc session state.
findings.gap: A looping caller can saturate the single server and its SQL Server instance.
findings.recommendation: Enforce per-principal request rate limits at an edge proxy or gateway.

findings.title: Blast Radius and Transaction Limits
findings.description: No business-domain caps exist - no maximum entries per session, no hours ceiling, no bulk-size limit. txtHours.Text is interpolated into the SQL numeric position with no bound check.
findings.gap: No limit on the number or magnitude of writes a single caller can produce.
findings.recommendation: Add configurable per-principal write quotas and database range constraints on hours.

findings.title: Draft/Pending State
findings.description: The insert writes only employee_id, entry_date, hours, and project - there is no status column and no create-then-confirm sequence. Every write commits immediately.
findings.gap: No reviewable intermediate state for a proposed entry.
findings.recommendation: Add a status field with a DRAFT/SUBMITTED lifecycle.

findings.title: Configurable Approval Gates
findings.description: No approval endpoint, confirmation step, or operation-level flag exists; btnSave_Click is the terminal action.
findings.gap: No per-operation human approval can be configured.
findings.recommendation: Introduce an approval workflow for agent-originated writes.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Classification
findings.description: Employee-attributable timesheet records are persisted in SQL Server. BindGrid() binds the raw DataTable from a SELECT directly to gridEntries with no DTO, field exclusion, or projection control, so consumers receive whatever columns the query returns. Authorization is a single role-less Forms-auth session, and no classification tags or field annotations exist.
findings.gap: No response-scoping layer between the database and the consumer, and no sensitive vs non-sensitive access differentiation.
findings.recommendation: Replace raw DataTable binding with explicit DTOs enumerating allowed fields, and add scoped permissions for employee-identifying fields.

findings.title: Data Residency and Sovereignty
findings.description: Employee timesheet data (worker-attributable labour records) is stored on a single fixed-IP SQL Server (Data Source=10.0.6.15). No residency policy, region configuration, replication boundary, or GDPR/LGPD reference appears in web.config or README.md.
findings.gap: No declared or enforced residency boundary, so there is no basis for deciding whether this data may be sent to an out-of-region model endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Document the jurisdiction and residency classification of the Timesheets database and enforce egress constraints.

findings.title: PII Redaction in Logs
findings.description: customErrors mode=Off combined with debug=true renders a full ASP.NET error page on failure, including the concatenated SQL text that embeds Session("EmployeeId"), txtDate.Text, and txtProject.Text. No masking or scrubbing exists.
findings.gap: Employee-attributable values are exposed in error output with no redaction.
findings.recommendation: Set customErrors mode=On and debug=false, then add structured logging with field-level PII masking.

findings.title: Identity Propagation and Delegation
findings.description: src/server.ts reads event.requestContext.authorizer.jwt.claims but keeps only the scope claim, building scopes: new Set(...). The sub, client_id, and any act/on-behalf-of claims are discarded, so resolvers cannot distinguish an agent calling under its own service identity from an agent calling on behalf of a specific human user — both arrive as an indistinguishable bag of scopes. There is no token exchange, no on-behalf-of flow, and no user-context propagation.
findings.gap: No actor/subject separation. An agent acting for a low-privilege user is bounded only by the agent's own scopes, not by that user's permissions.
findings.recommendation: Propagate sub and client_id into the resolver Context, add an explicit actingOnBehalfOf field populated from an act claim or a token-validated X-On-Behalf-Of-User header, and enforce the intersection of agent scopes and user permissions in requireScope.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: Neither mutation resolver records the authenticated principal. upsertProduct and deleteProduct in src/resolvers/catalog.ts call ctx.db.put / ctx.db.update and return immediately — no log statement, no audit record, and no actor attribute on the item (only updatedAt). src/server.ts extracts JWT claims but discards sub and client_id, so the principal is not even available to a downstream audit writer. infra/template.yaml contains no AWS::CloudTrail::Trail, no log-file validation, no S3 Object Lock log target, and no CloudWatch log-group retention policy; the only observability configured is sampled X-Ray tracing. README.md acknowledges the gap narrowly for deleteProduct; it is in fact total across both write paths.
findings.gap: No principal attribution on any write operation and no immutable or tamper-evident log store. Agent-initiated mutations cannot be attributed or forensically reconstructed.
findings.recommendation: Carry claims.sub and claims.client_id into the resolver context and emit a structured audit record (principal, operation, SKU, before/after active, timestamp, request id) per write to a dedicated CloudWatch log group or DynamoDB audit table; add a CloudTrail trail with LogFileValidationEnabled and DynamoDB data events delivering to an S3 bucket with Object Lock.

findings.title: Concurrency Controls
findings.description: upsertProduct issues an unconditional ctx.db.put with no ConditionExpression, no version attribute, and no If-Match/ETag equivalent in the GraphQL schema; deleteProduct issues an unconditional update SET active = :f. The Product type in schema/catalog.graphql exposes updatedAt but no version field, so a caller has no token to condition on. Two concurrent agent instances upserting the same SKU produce silent last-writer-wins, and a concurrent upsert and soft-delete can resurrect a deleted product.
findings.gap: No optimistic locking on a write surface an agent may drive concurrently at machine speed.
findings.recommendation: Add a version: Int! attribute to Product and UpsertProductInput and convert both mutations to DynamoDB conditional writes (ConditionExpression: 'attribute_not_exists(sku) OR version = :expected'), returning a structured conflict error on failure.

findings.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
findings.description: The CatalogApi HTTP API in infra/template.yaml declares only Auth — no RouteSettings/DefaultRouteSettings with ThrottlingBurstLimit or ThrottlingRateLimit, no usage plan, no WAF web ACL — and package.json declares no rate-limiting middleware or Apollo rate-limit plugin. Compounding this, src/server.ts installs no query depth or complexity limit, so a single deeply nested GraphQL document is both unthrottled and unbounded in cost; README.md and the src/server.ts header comment both acknowledge this.
findings.gap: A runaway agent loop, or one expensive query, can exhaust Lambda concurrency and DynamoDB on-demand capacity with nothing in front of it.
findings.recommendation: Add DefaultRouteSettings throttling to CatalogApi and install graphql-depth-limit plus an Apollo cost-analysis plugin in src/server.ts as the file's own header comment prescribes.

findings.title: Blast Radius and Transaction Limits
findings.description: No business-domain caps exist for any caller. schema/catalog.graphql exposes only single-SKU mutations (no bulk upsert or bulk delete), which caps one call, but nothing caps a session: an agent can call deleteProduct once per SKU in a loop and soft-delete the entire catalog. There is no per-identity maximum records modified, no mutations-per-hour ceiling, and no spend threshold. On the read side products(limit: Int = 50) has a default but no enforced maximum — limit is passed straight through to the DynamoDB Limit in src/resolvers/catalog.ts.
findings.gap: Only per-operation scope is bounded; cumulative per-caller business impact is unbounded. API-layer throttling (also absent) would bound request rate, not business consequence.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-principal mutation budget (e.g., a DynamoDB counter keyed on client_id and hour, checked in requireScope or a dedicated guard) and clamp limit in the products resolver to a hard maximum.

findings.title: Draft/Pending State
findings.description: Product in schema/catalog.graphql carries a two-valued active: Boolean! and nothing else resembling a lifecycle state — no status enum, no DRAFT/PENDING_REVIEW value, no separate staging table. upsertProduct in src/resolvers/catalog.ts hardcodes active: true on every write, so a write is live the instant it commits, and there is no create-then-confirm operation pair. active: false is a delete marker, not a reviewable pre-commit state.
findings.gap: No mechanism for an agent to propose a catalog change without immediately publishing it.
findings.recommendation: Replace active: Boolean! with a status: ProductStatus! enum (DRAFT, PUBLISHED, ARCHIVED), default agent-originated upserts to DRAFT, and add a publishProduct(sku) mutation gated on a distinct scope.

findings.title: Configurable Approval Gates
findings.description: No approval surface exists. schema/catalog.graphql has exactly four operations (product, products, upsertProduct, deleteProduct) — no approve/reject mutation and no confirmation step. infra/template.yaml contains no Step Functions state machine (hence no waitForTaskToken human-approval task) and no per-operation feature flags or parameters. requireScope in src/resolvers/catalog.ts is a binary allow/deny on catalog:write and cannot route an operation to a human.
findings.gap: Operations cannot be configured to require human approval per operation type, so there is no application-layer defense in depth behind the orchestration layer.
findings.recommendation: Introduce an operation-level policy map (operation name → requires_approval) consulted in the resolvers, backed by the DRAFT/publishProduct split recommended for HITL-Q1 so gated operations have somewhere to park.

findings.title: Idempotent Write Operations
findings.description: settlement_writer performs an unconditional UPDATE claims SET status='SETTLED' followed by an INSERT INTO payment_queue. There is no idempotency key, no status precondition and no unique constraint, and agent.py dispatches whatever tool the model returns with no de-duplication, so a retried toolUse releases a second payment.
findings.gap: No idempotency key support, no conditional write, no duplicate-payment guard.
findings.recommendation: Add a required idempotency_key parameter with a unique constraint on payment_queue(claim_id, idempotency_key) and make the claims update conditional on current status.

findings.title: Machine Identity Authentication
findings.description: The MCP tool gateway is declared AuthorizerType: NONE, so any caller reaching the endpoint invokes any tool unauthenticated, and docs/security-review-TODO.md confirms the runtime ARN additionally accepts SigV4 from any principal in the account. The only caller identifier in code is --actor-id, a self-asserted CLI argument defaulting to adjuster-pool.
findings.gap: No authenticated machine identity and no principal attribution on the agent-facing surface.
findings.recommendation: Replace AuthorizerType: NONE with an AgentCore Identity / OAuth JWT authorizer and restrict the runtime resource policy to approved principals.

findings.title: Scoped Permissions (Least Privilege)
findings.description: infra/agent-iam.yaml defines one role, claims-agent-execution, shared by the AgentCore Runtime and the tool Lambda. Every statement uses Resource: '*' - Bedrock invoke, retrieval, memory, runtime invoke (including InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell), Secrets Manager and logs. The gateway role allows lambda:InvokeFunction on '*'.
findings.gap: No per-capability roles, no resource ARNs, no condition keys.
findings.recommendation: Issue one role per component with explicit resource ARNs and remove InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell from the agent role.

findings.title: Action-Level Authorization
findings.description: REGISTRY exposes load_claim, policy_lookup, payment_history and the money-moving settlement_writer as one flat set, and agent.py dispatches any of them with no capability check. docs/security-review-TODO.md confirms tools/list returns the full registry to every caller with no per-caller allow-list, and the single IAM role makes read and write tools indistinguishable.
findings.gap: No read-vs-write differentiation at the tool or gateway layer.
findings.recommendation: Enforce a per-principal tool allow-list before dispatch and move settlement_writer behind its own gateway target and role.

findings.title: Identity Propagation and Delegation
findings.description: triage(claim_id, actor_id) takes actor_id as an unauthenticated argument defaulting to adjuster-pool, and that value is used directly as the AgentCore Memory actor key. No JWT parsing, token exchange or on-behalf-of flow exists, and all DB access uses one shared claims/db/readwrite credential, so agent-as-self and agent-on-behalf-of-user are indistinguishable.
findings.gap: No verified caller identity propagated through the agent, tools or memory.
findings.recommendation: Derive actor_id from a gateway-verified token and propagate it as the memory actor and the DB session identity.

findings.title: Credential Management
findings.description: DB credentials are correctly fetched from Secrets Manager at call time and no hardcoded passwords were found in source, IaC or config. However secretsmanager:GetSecretValue is granted on Resource: '*', so a prompt-injection or tool compromise reads every secret in the account, and no RotationSchedule exists for the read-write claims credential.
findings.gap: No rotation schedule; secret read permission is unbounded.
findings.recommendation: Add a managed rotation schedule and scope the secret ARN; split read-only and read-write DB secrets.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: No CloudTrail trail, log file validation or S3 Object Lock appears in infra/. The only sink is ClaimsTranscriptLogs, a mutable CloudWatch log group fed by runtime stdout with 3653-day retention. settlement_writer records no principal on the money-moving write, and docs/security-review-TODO.md confirms an end-to-end session cannot be reconstructed.
findings.gap: No immutable, tamper-evident audit trail attributing write operations to a principal.
findings.recommendation: Enable CloudTrail with log file validation for bedrock and bedrock-agentcore events and persist a principal/session id on every claims and payment_queue mutation.

findings.title: Agent Identity Suspension
findings.description: One identity covers everything: claims-agent-execution is assumed by both the runtime and the tool Lambda, and the gateway has no authorizer, so there are no per-agent credentials to revoke. Disabling the shared role takes down the whole triage service including the attended adjuster path. No key revocation or identity disable mechanism exists in code or IaC.
findings.gap: No way to isolate a misbehaving agent identity without a full outage.
findings.recommendation: Issue one revocable machine identity per agent deployment behind the gateway authorizer.

findings.title: Compensation and Rollback
findings.description: settlement_writer commits a two-statement sequence (claims status update plus payment_queue insert) and returns; there is no saga, compensating transaction or undo tool in REGISTRY. docs/batch-mode.md states rollback is manual - pull the payment_queue rows for the run and reverse them - while batch mode settles up to 500 claims per run.
findings.gap: No automated compensation for failed or erroneous multi-step settlement sequences.
findings.recommendation: Add a settlement_reversal operation and gate payment release behind a separate confirmed step so a partial failure can be reversed programmatically.

findings.title: Concurrency Controls
findings.description: settlement_writer issues UPDATE claims SET status='SETTLED' ... WHERE claim_id=%s with no version column, no SELECT FOR UPDATE and no status precondition. Batch mode runs concurrently with the attended adjuster path, so two runs can settle the same claim and insert two payment_queue rows.
findings.gap: No optimistic or pessimistic locking on the settlement write path.
findings.recommendation: Make the settle statement conditional on the expected current status and assert rowcount == 1.

findings.title: Circuit Breakers and Resilience
findings.description: All four downstream clients use bare defaults - boto3 clients for bedrock-runtime, bedrock-agentcore and bedrock-agent-runtime, plus psycopg2.connect with no connect_timeout. No botocore Config retry/timeout settings, no backoff and no circuit breaker exist, and requirements.txt declares no resilience library; a slow dependency stalls the 60-second tool Lambda.
findings.gap: No timeouts, retry policy or circuit breaking on external dependency calls.
findings.recommendation: Centralise client construction with explicit botocore Config timeouts, bounded retries and a breaker around the DB tools.

findings.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
findings.description: ClaimsToolGateway and ClaimsAgentRuntime declare no throttle settings, usage plan or WAF association, and ClaimsToolFunction has no reserved concurrency. No application-level rate limiting middleware exists in src/claims_agent/. With NetworkMode: PUBLIC and no authorizer, a runaway tool loop is bounded only by Bedrock service quotas.
findings.gap: No request-rate protection on the agent-facing surface.
findings.recommendation: Add per-caller throttling at the gateway and reserved concurrency on the tool Lambda.

findings.title: Blast Radius and Transaction Limits
findings.description: settlement_writer accepts any amount float and writes it as-is with no ceiling, per-session spend cap or per-identity limit. docs/batch-mode.md states there is no approval step and no dollar ceiling, and that the auto-approve threshold check lives in the UI so batch mode bypasses it. The only bound is the operator-supplied --max-claims 500 CLI flag.
findings.gap: No business-domain cap on settled amount, payments per run or spend per session.
findings.recommendation: Move the auto-approve threshold into settlement_writer and enforce per-run payment count and cumulative-amount ceilings from configuration.

findings.title: Draft/Pending State
findings.description: The only status the agent writes is terminal: status='SETTLED' plus an immediate INSERT INTO payment_queue with released_at = now() in the same committed transaction. No DRAFT/PENDING/PROPOSED state, create-then-confirm pair or approval operation exists in REGISTRY, even though README.md states the adjuster is expected to review every recommendation.
findings.gap: No reviewable intermediate state between agent proposal and payment release.
findings.recommendation: Split settlement_writer into propose_settlement (agent, writes PENDING_REVIEW) and commit_settlement (human-triggered).

findings.title: Configurable Approval Gates
findings.description: No approval operation, operation-level flag or waitForTaskToken wait state exists in src/claims_agent/ or infra/. docs/batch-mode.md documents unattended runs draining the queue without an adjuster in the loop, with the human-queue routing check implemented in the UI only and therefore bypassed. The system prompt further instructs the model to recommend approval for routine claims.
findings.gap: No application-layer approval gate configurable by operation type or amount.
findings.recommendation: Implement a server-side approval gate keyed on operation type and settlement amount, and disable batch mode until it exists.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Classification
findings.description: Stage A = Yes: the system reads SSNs and bank routing numbers from Postgres. load_claim selects and returns claimant_ssn and payment_history returns routing_no and account_last4 in general-purpose tool responses, both of which land in the model prompt and in AgentCore Memory. No serializer exclusion, projection or separate DTO filters these fields, a single shared role grants all data access, and no classification metadata exists anywhere in the repo.
findings.gap: Sensitive fields are returned unscoped to the model, with no access differentiation and no classification metadata.
findings.recommendation: Remove claimant_ssn and routing_no from the tool SELECT projections, returning a tokenised or last-4 form only where needed for matching.

findings.title: Data Residency and Sovereignty
findings.description: The execution role allows bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:Converse on Resource: '*' and MODEL_ID is an unvalidated environment variable, so claim text containing SSNs can be sent to any model enabled in the account, including cross-region inference profiles. No residency constraint, region condition key, GDPR/LGPD reference or sovereignty policy exists, and AgentCore Memory retains the raw exchange for 365 days with no jurisdictional scoping.
findings.gap: No region or jurisdiction constraint on where regulated claims data is transmitted or retained.
findings.recommendation: Scope bedrock invoke actions to approved in-region model ARNs with an aws:RequestedRegion condition and pin CLAIMS_MODEL_ID to a reviewed allow-list.

findings.title: PII Redaction in Logs
findings.description: agent.py logs the full prompt, the full completion and every tool result at INFO level, and those payloads contain claimant_ssn from load_claim and routing_no from payment_history. There is no scrubbing middleware, no masking dependency, and no CloudWatch data-protection policy on ClaimsTranscriptLogs, which retains for 3653 days. memory.remember additionally persists the raw exchange into AgentCore Memory unredacted.
findings.gap: PII and bank details written verbatim to a 10-year mutable log and to long-term memory.
findings.recommendation: Stop selecting the sensitive fields at source, add a log-scrubbing layer and a CloudWatch data-protection policy, and shorten retention.

findings.title: Idempotent Write Operations
findings.description: No idempotency mechanism exists on any write endpoint. `POST /orders/:id/refund` in src/routes.ts calls OrderService.refund(), which issues a real money movement through WarehouseClient.issueRefund() with no Idempotency-Key handling, no request de-duplication store, and no unique business-key constraint. `POST /orders` and `DELETE /orders/:id` are likewise non-idempotent. openapi/orders.yaml documents the gap explicitly ('No Idempotency-Key - a duplicate call double-refunds'), and SAFETY.md lists it as an unremediated control gap.
findings.gap: No Idempotency-Key header accepted, no de-duplication table, no conditional write or unique constraint on refund/order creation. An agent retrying a timed-out refund double-refunds the customer.
findings.recommendation: Accept and require an `Idempotency-Key` header on POST /orders, POST /orders/:id/refund and POST /orders/:id/cancel. Persist the key with the request hash and the first response in a `request_idempotency` table with a unique index, and replay the stored response on repeat. Pass the same key through to the payment processor so the downstream call is idempotent too.

findings.title: Action-Level Authorization
findings.description: Authorization is role-coarse, not action-level. src/routes.ts guards POST /orders, DELETE /orders/:id, POST /orders/:id/refund and POST /orders/:id/cancel all with the single `requireRole('orders:write')` check. src/auth.ts implements exactly one primitive - membership of a required role string in the `roles` claim. There is no canRead/canWrite/canDelete separation, no ABAC conditions, and no per-operation permission matrix.
findings.gap: A caller granted `orders:write` so it can create an order automatically also inherits hard-delete, refund and warehouse-recall authority. There is no way to issue an agent identity that may update orders but not delete them or move money.
findings.recommendation: Split `orders:write` into per-action scopes (`orders:create`, `orders:refund`, `orders:cancel`, `orders:delete`) and change each route's preHandler to require the specific scope. Keep the irreversible actions (delete, refund, cancel) behind their own scopes so an agent identity can be issued the non-destructive subset.

findings.title: Identity Propagation and Delegation
findings.description: src/auth.ts verifies the inbound JWT (issuer, audience orders-service, RS256 via remote JWKS) but does not propagate it: the payload is read for the roles claim and then discarded, and OrderService receives only primitive arguments. Downstream calls to WarehouseClient.issueRefund()/recallDispatch() in src/services/order-service.ts carry no identity, no token exchange, and no on-behalf-of context. There is no distinction anywhere between a principal acting as itself and a principal acting on behalf of a named human user.
findings.gap: No identity propagation to downstream systems and no agent-as-self vs agent-on-behalf-of-user differentiation. The warehouse/payment dependency must trust all calls from this service equally, and an agent's effective authority cannot be bounded by the authority of the user it is acting for.
findings.recommendation: Attach the verified payload to the Fastify request, pass a caller-context object into OrderService, and forward a propagated or exchanged token on the warehouse/payment calls. Add distinct claims (or distinct audiences) for agent-as-self vs user-delegated calls, and record the mode on the audit record from AUTH-Q6.

findings.title: Immutable Audit Logging
findings.description: The authenticated principal is never recorded for write operations. src/auth.ts verifies the RS256 JWT and checks the role claim but discards the payload - it is not attached to the request, not logged, and not passed into OrderService. No route in src/routes.ts writes an audit record, and OrderService.hardDelete() deletes the row with no audit trail (SAFETY.md: 'No soft-delete, no audit, no confirmation'). infra/ecs.yaml configures only an awslogs driver to log group /ecs/orders with no retention policy; there is no CloudTrail resource, no log-file validation, and no S3 Object Lock or other tamper-evident store.
findings.gap: No per-write audit record attributing the action to a principal, and no immutable/tamper-evident log storage. Agent-initiated refunds, cancellations and hard deletes would be indistinguishable from human actions and unreconstructable after the fact.
findings.recommendation: Attach the verified JWT payload (sub, client_id, roles, jti) to the Fastify request in src/auth.ts, and emit an append-only audit record for every mutating operation containing principal, operation, target order id, before/after status and request id. Ship audit records to a dedicated store with immutability guarantees (S3 with Object Lock, or CloudWatch Logs with a retention policy plus CloudTrail data events) and set a retention policy on /ecs/orders.

findings.title: Agent Identity Suspension
findings.description: There is no revocation or suspension path in the repository. src/auth.ts validates tokens statelessly against a remote JWKS (createRemoteJWKSet) with no denylist check, no jti/introspection lookup, no token TTL policy, and no per-client enable/disable flag. There are no API keys to revoke (no API Gateway usage plan in infra/ecs.yaml) and no IAM-based caller identity to deactivate - the only identity control point is the external issuer, which is not configured in this repo.
findings.gap: A misbehaving agent identity cannot be cut off at the service: an already-issued JWT remains accepted until it expires, and the only lever is disabling the client at the identity provider or taking the whole service down.
findings.recommendation: Add a revocation check to the auth middleware - a cached denylist of revoked jti/client_id values (or token introspection) refreshed on a short interval - plus a per-client kill switch in configuration. Keep access-token lifetimes short so revocation latency is bounded.

findings.title: Compensation and Rollback
findings.description: No compensation or rollback exists for the multi-step write sequences. OrderService.refund() first runs `UPDATE orders SET status='refunded'` and then calls this.warehouse.issueRefund(); OrderService.cancelAndRecallShipment() runs `UPDATE orders SET status='cancelled'` and then calls this.warehouse.recallDispatch(). Neither pair is wrapped in a transaction, and neither has a compensating action if the second step fails. There is no saga coordinator, no Step Functions definition, and no undo endpoint anywhere in the repository.
findings.gap: If the downstream warehouse/payment call fails after the local UPDATE commits, the order is permanently marked refunded/cancelled while no money moved and no dispatch was recalled - a silent partial state with no reconciliation path. OrderService.hardDelete() is irreversible by construction (no soft-delete column).
findings.recommendation: Wrap each mutation plus its downstream effect in an outbox or saga pattern: write a pending intent row in the same local transaction as the status change, dispatch the downstream call from a worker, and define an explicit compensating action (revert status, re-issue dispatch) for each failure branch. Replace hardDelete with a soft-delete column so delete is compensable.

findings.title: Concurrency Controls
findings.description: No concurrency control exists. OrderService.refund() and cancelAndRecallShipment() issue unconditional `UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2` statements with no version column, no status precondition in the WHERE clause, no SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, and no ETag/If-Match support in src/routes.ts. The Order interface in src/services/order-service.ts has no version or updated_at field.
findings.gap: Two concurrent agent instances can both refund or both cancel the same order: each UPDATE succeeds and each downstream warehouse/payment call fires, double-refunding or double-recalling. Lost-update and double-side-effect races are unprotected.
findings.recommendation: Add a `version` (or `updated_at`) column to orders and make every mutation a conditional update - `UPDATE orders SET status=$1, version=version+1 WHERE id=$2 AND version=$3` - returning 409 when zero rows are affected. Also add status preconditions (only a `placed`/`shipped` order may be refunded) and expose the version as an ETag with If-Match on the mutating routes.

findings.title: Circuit Breakers and Resilience
findings.description: The service calls two external dependencies - PostgreSQL via the pg Pool and WarehouseClient (payment processor and warehouse dispatch) - with no resilience controls. src/services/order-service.ts awaits this.warehouse.issueRefund() and this.warehouse.recallDispatch() directly with no timeout, no retry policy, no bounded backoff and no circuit breaker. package.json declares no resilience library (no cockatiel, opossum, undici retry config), the pg Pool is constructed without connectionTimeoutMillis/statement_timeout, and the only circuit breaker in infra/ecs.yaml is the ECS DeploymentCircuitBreaker, which governs deployments, not dependency calls.
findings.gap: A slow or failing warehouse/payment dependency propagates straight back to the caller as a hung request. Combined with agent-speed retries this produces connection exhaustion and amplified load on the downstream dependency, with no breaker to shed it.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the WarehouseClient calls with an explicit timeout, bounded exponential-backoff retry restricted to idempotent operations, and a circuit breaker that fails fast with a structured retriable error. Set connectionTimeoutMillis and statement_timeout on the pg Pool.

findings.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling
