Authorization is entirely coarse-grained: there is no mechanism to grant an agent identity narrower access than 'may submit orders as any partner through the shared database account'. Scoping down an agent is not possible without new code.
There is no mechanism to grant a caller read-only access to a subset of payroll data. Any identity that can run or read this job inherits the full surface.
No capability to differentiate access levels per caller. An agent identity cannot be constrained to a subset of SKUs, endpoints, or operations; it inherits the full surface by default.

All authorization is effectively absent, which is the extreme case of coarse-grained: there is no mechanism to grant an agent read-only access to orders without also granting order creation and card charging. Blast radius cannot be scoped down.
No mechanism exists to grant a read-only, resource-scoped identity.
No per-capability roles, no resource ARNs, no condition keys.

items.common_finding_summary: Sensitive values reach logs unredacted — request bodies, query parameters, claimant and employee records are written to log sinks with no masking or data-protection policy.
items.root_cause_pattern: CloudWatch Logs data-protection policies with managed PII identifiers; a shared redaction helper applied before any log write; guardrail sensitive-information filters on model paths.
items.remediation: Apply a CloudWatch Logs data-protection policy to every agent-path log group and add a shared redaction utility to the logging layer, so agent-driven traffic volume does not multiply PII exposure.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Apply a CloudWatch Logs data-protection policy to every agent-path log group and add a shared redaction utility to the logging layer, so agent-driven traffic volume does not multiply PII exposure.
remediation_detail.target_state: Apply a CloudWatch Logs data-protection policy to every agent-path log group and add a shared redaction utility to the logging layer, so agent-driven traffic volume does not multiply PII exposure.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: No redaction control exists for a system that handles customer PII, so any future or operational logging (including crash dumps and the nightly sync job) carries unmasked personal data into observable surfaces.

User search terms and user identities reach error output through an uncontrolled path, with no redaction, no structured logging to apply redaction to, and no control over who sees the resulting error pages.
There is no redaction layer, so PII entered into search queries and present in exception context is persisted to host log files with no retention or access control.
No redaction control exists on the one path that does emit user data — stack traces and SQL text containing applicant PII reach container logs in the clear.

Partner business data and infrastructure detail can leak into error responses and into container logs with no redaction layer. The surface-flag INFO downgrade does not apply because the system holds user/partner data (has_persistent_data_store = true).
Employee SSNs and bank account numbers sit in the working record area with no masking policy, so abend dumps and spool output are an uncontrolled PII egress path.

Full card numbers and customer details can land in plaintext application logs on the EC2 hosts, with no masking and (per AUTH-Q6) no controlled retention — a PCI exposure that widens as agents drive request volume.
Employee-attributable values are exposed in error output with no redaction.
PII and bank details written verbatim to a 10-year mutable log and to long-term memory.

Order rows containing customer PII can reach CloudWatch unredacted via request/response or error logging, and the log group has no retention limit, so any leakage is retained indefinitely. There is no configured redaction path at all.

items.common_finding_summary: No service has a configurable approval gate. Thresholds that would warrant human review — settlement amount, refund value, payroll run, bulk delete — are not expressed anywhere in code or config.
items.root_cause_pattern: Threshold-driven approval workflow (Step Functions callback pattern or equivalent) in front of high-impact operations; thresholds in configuration, not code.
items.remediation: Define portfolio approval thresholds per operation class and implement one shared approval gate component, wired first into the money-moving and bulk-mutation paths.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Define portfolio approval thresholds per operation class and implement one shared approval gate component, wired first into the money-moving and bulk-mutation paths.
remediation_detail.target_state: Define portfolio approval thresholds per operation class and implement one shared approval gate component, wired first into the money-moving and bulk-mutation paths.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: High-risk operations cannot be configured to require human approval at the application layer, so there is no defense-in-depth beneath whatever gate the orchestration layer provides.
High-risk operations (loan submission) cannot be configured to require human approval at the application layer, so the only possible gate is outside the system.
High-value or unusual agent submissions cannot be routed through human approval at the application layer; the service has no concept of an operation requiring confirmation.
High-impact operations (generating and transmitting a payroll disbursement file) cannot be configured to require human approval at the system layer; the only control is the scheduler.
High-risk operations — order creation with a live card charge — cannot be configured to require human approval, so there is no application-layer defence in depth for an agent-initiated payment.
No per-operation human approval can be configured.
Operations cannot be configured to require human approval per operation type, so there is no application-layer defense in depth behind the orchestration layer.
No application-layer approval gate configurable by operation type or amount.

High-risk operations - a real refund, a physical dispatch recall and a hard delete of customer PII - execute autonomously on a single API call with no application-layer human checkpoint and no configurable threshold above which review is required.
High-risk operations (large refunds in particular) cannot be configured to require human approval before execution, so there is no defense-in-depth below the orchestration layer.

items.common_finding_summary: No concurrency control exists on agent-writable state: no optimistic version checks, no conditional writes, no row locking. Two concurrent agent writes silently last-write-wins.
items.root_cause_pattern: DynamoDB condition expressions / `ConditionCheck`, SQL optimistic locking with a version column, and ETag/If-Match on HTTP mutations.
items.remediation: Require an optimistic-concurrency token (version column or ETag) on every agent-writable resource, so concurrent agent writes fail loudly rather than overwriting each other.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Require an optimistic-concurrency token (version column or ETag) on every agent-writable resource, so concurrent agent writes fail loudly rather than overwriting each other.
remediation_detail.target_state: Require an optimistic-concurrency token (version column or ETag) on every agent-writable resource, so concurrent agent writes fail loudly rather than overwriting each other.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: Concurrent writers corrupt the data file — an already-observed monthly failure. Multiple concurrent agent instances would multiply write contention on a store with no locking discipline.
Concurrent callers can interleave on shared mutable form state and create duplicate or inconsistent application rows; the documented thread-safety defect is amplified by machine-speed concurrency.
Nothing prevents two concurrent agent instances (or an agent racing a human partner) from booking the same purchase order twice, and there is no conflict signal the agent could react to.
Concurrent invocations can read the employee master mid-update and produce divergent or duplicated payout files; there is no conflict detection to reject the second writer.
Concurrent agent instances creating or updating orders can interleave without detection, producing duplicate orders and lost updates — compounded by the absence of idempotency keys (API-Q4).
Concurrent callers can create conflicting or duplicate entries for the same employee and date.
No optimistic locking on a write surface an agent may drive concurrently at machine speed.
No optimistic or pessimistic locking on the settlement write path.

Two concurrent agent instances can both refund or both cancel the same order: each UPDATE succeeds and each downstream warehouse/payment call fires, double-refunding or double-recalling. Lost-update and double-side-effect races are unprotected.

Read-then-write with no conditional write leaves a race window: two concurrent agent retries carrying the same Idempotency-Key can both pass the get_item check and both write ledger rows, which is exactly the duplicate-charge case idempotency is meant to prevent.

items.common_finding_summary: Nothing bounds the blast radius of a single agent operation: no row caps on bulk updates, no per-transaction value limits, no maximum batch size.
items.root_cause_pattern: Hard server-side caps on batch size and transaction value; a daily per-agent operation budget; mandatory pagination on list/bulk endpoints.
items.remediation: Set server-side blast-radius caps (max rows per mutation, max value per transaction, max operations per agent per day) as a portfolio default rather than a per-service choice.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Set server-side blast-radius caps (max rows per mutation, max value per transaction, max operations per agent per day) as a portfolio default rather than a per-service choice.
remediation_detail.target_state: Set server-side blast-radius caps (max rows per mutation, max value per transaction, max operations per agent per day) as a portfolio default rather than a per-service choice.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: There is no way to cap the blast radius of a caller executing correct-but-catastrophic logic — e.g. inserting thousands of customer rows into a file store that corrupts under write pressure.
The business impact of an erroneous agent loop is unbounded: it could submit an unlimited number of loan applications at arbitrary principal and rate values.
The blast radius of an agent error is unbounded in business terms: an agent loop could book an arbitrary number of orders at arbitrary values, and nothing in the system would stop or flag it.
A single invocation can generate payout records for every employee with no cap on record count or total monetary value, so an erroneous agent-initiated run has unbounded financial blast radius.

There is no ceiling on the business impact of a correct-but-catastrophic agent loop. An agent repeatedly invoking `create` can issue unlimited live charges; nothing bounds spend per session or records touched per run.
No limit on the number or magnitude of writes a single caller can produce.
Only per-operation scope is bounded; cumulative per-caller business impact is unbounded. API-layer throttling (also absent) would bound request rate, not business consequence.
No business-domain cap on settled amount, payments per run or spend per session.

The blast radius of an agent error is unbounded: a looping agent could refund an arbitrary total value or hard-delete every order it can enumerate, and nothing in the system would stop it before the damage was done. The only protection contemplated is request-rate throttling (also absent - STATE-Q5), which does not cap business impact.
A correct-but-catastrophic agent loop — refunding every charge it reads — is not stopped by any business limit. Throttling alone (once added, STATE-Q5) limits request rate, not refunded value.

items.common_finding_summary: When an agent acts for a user, the user's identity is not propagated. Services either run entirely as the application principal or forward no on-behalf-of context, so downstream decisions and logs cannot see the human.
items.root_cause_pattern: On-behalf-of token exchange at the identity plane; an `act` / delegation claim carried on every agent call and surfaced into audit records.
items.remediation: Standardise one delegation claim across the portfolio and require it on any agent call made on a user's behalf; never forward the user's raw token to a downstream tool.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Standardise one delegation claim across the portfolio and require it on any agent call made on a user's behalf; never forward the user's raw token to a downstream tool.
remediation_detail.target_state: Standardise one delegation claim across the portfolio and require it on any agent call made on a user's behalf; never forward the user's raw token to a downstream tool.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: An agent acting on behalf of a user cannot be bounded by that user's permissions, and the `CreatedBy` attribution it writes is caller-asserted and unverifiable.
An agent acting on behalf of a loan officer cannot be bounded by that officer's permissions, and the audit column cannot separate actor from subject.

Agent-as-self and agent-on-behalf-of-partner are indistinguishable, and the subject of the operation (which partner the order is booked against) is attacker-controllable - a privilege-escalation path by construction.

The system cannot distinguish an agent acting as itself from an agent acting on behalf of a specific user, and no caller identity survives the FTP hop to the EC2 gateway — the gateway sees only the shared account.

The system cannot distinguish an agent acting under its own service identity from an agent acting on behalf of a specific customer, and cannot bound the latter by that customer's permissions — a privilege-escalation path for any on-behalf-of agent workflow.
On-behalf-of flows are impossible; a caller would have to assume a human's session.
No actor/subject separation. An agent acting for a low-privilege user is bounded only by the agent's own scopes, not by that user's permissions.
No verified caller identity propagated through the agent, tools or memory.

No identity propagation to downstream systems and no agent-as-self vs agent-on-behalf-of-user differentiation. The warehouse/payment dependency must trust all calls from this service equally, and an agent's effective authority cannot be bounded by the authority of the user it is acting for.

items.common_finding_summary: Credentials are embedded or statically configured: connection strings in source and config (legacy services), long-lived static secrets, and no rotation anywhere. No service reads its credential from a managed secret store at runtime.
items.root_cause_pattern: AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation; short-lived tokens from the shared IdP instead of static keys; no plaintext credential in any repository.
items.remediation: Move every agent-path credential into Secrets Manager with rotation enabled, and replace static service keys with short-lived client-credentials tokens.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Move every agent-path credential into Secrets Manager with rotation enabled, and replace static service keys with short-lived client-credentials tokens.
remediation_detail.target_state: Move every agent-path credential into Secrets Manager with rotation enabled, and replace static service keys with short-lived client-credentials tokens.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: A static, unrotated, shared credential is embedded in code and in every deployed EXE. Anything that can read the binary or the repository — including a prompt-injected agent with file access — obtains full database access.

A weak, documented, never-rotated administrator credential is recorded in the repository itself. Any caller — including an agent with access to repository content or to the README — can read it, and there is no rotation path that would limit the exposure window.

No secrets manager, no rotation, and no environment indirection. Any repository reader obtains database access, and the static SECRET_KEY allows session/signature forgery. Prompt-injection or a verbose error path could surface these values to an agent.

A static, unrotated production database password is committed to version control and duplicated in the deployment artifact — exactly the kind of secret an agent-facing surface or prompt-injection path can exfiltrate.

Credentials are committed to version control, shared, and unrotatable without a code change and redeploy. The password value is embedded in a compiled artifact, so rotation requires a release. This is severe evidence on a RISK-SAFETY question: a prompt-injection or error-leak path (see DATA-Q6) could expose the connection string.
A long-lived plaintext credential for the payroll transfer account is readable by anyone with repository access and is present in git history. No rotation mechanism exists.

Production payment credentials are readable by anyone with repository access and persist in git history, with no rotation path. An agent bug or prompt-injection that can read application config or echo file contents can exfiltrate a live merchant credential.
A static, shared, plaintext production credential committed to source control with no rotation.
No rotation schedule; secret read permission is unbounded.

items.common_finding_summary: Mutating operations commit immediately. There is no draft, pending or proposed state an agent could write into for a human to confirm — the write is the decision.
items.root_cause_pattern: A `pending` status plus a confirm/reject transition on mutating resources; agent writes land in pending by default.
items.remediation: Add a draft/pending state to every mutating agent-callable resource and make `pending` the default outcome of an agent-initiated write during pilot.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Add a draft/pending state to every mutating agent-callable resource and make `pending` the default outcome of an agent-initiated write during pilot.
remediation_detail.target_state: Add a draft/pending state to every mutating agent-callable resource and make `pending` the default outcome of an agent-initiated write during pilot.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: Every write is immediately final, so a proposed change cannot be staged for human review before it becomes authoritative data.
An agent cannot propose a loan application for human review — any write it makes is final on first call.
An agent cannot propose an order for human review; every agent write is immediately committed as accepted, with no reviewable intermediate state and (per STATE-Q1) no way to reverse it.
There is no reviewable intermediate state between calculation and disbursement, so a proposed payroll run cannot be inspected and approved before it is committed and transmitted.
No reviewable intermediate state for a proposed entry.
No mechanism for an agent to propose a catalog change without immediately publishing it.
No reviewable intermediate state between agent proposal and payment release.

An agent cannot propose a refund, cancellation or deletion for review - every write it makes is immediately committed and, for the three irreversible operations, cannot be undone. There is no reviewable intermediate state to repurpose for agent-initiated proposals.
Every agent-initiated write commits immediately. The 'pending' enum value cannot be used as a proposal state because no transition endpoint exists to move pending to succeeded.

items.common_finding_summary: Calls to dependencies have no timeout, retry budget or circuit breaker, so a slow dependency becomes an unbounded queue of agent-initiated work.
items.root_cause_pattern: Shared client wrapper with timeouts, bounded retries with jitter, and a circuit breaker; bulkheads/reserved concurrency per caller class.
items.remediation: Publish one resilience client wrapper (timeout + bounded retry + breaker) and require its use on every outbound call on an agent-reachable path.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Publish one resilience client wrapper (timeout + bounded retry + breaker) and require its use on every outbound call on an agent-reachable path.
remediation_detail.target_state: Publish one resilience client wrapper (timeout + bounded retry + breaker) and require its use on every outbound call on an agent-reachable path.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: A slow or unavailable file share produces an unhandled failure or an indefinite hang, and repeated caller retries apply unbounded pressure to a dependency with no failover.

A slow or unavailable PostgreSQL or Exchange relay causes requests to hang on Apache's worker threads with no circuit breaker, so agent-speed traffic can exhaust the single instance and cascade failures back to the caller.

A slow or unavailable dependency (DB2, the EC2 gateway) produces an abend or a silent partial result rather than a bounded, retried, circuit-broken failure — and an agent calling in would observe no distinction.
A slow or failing payment gateway blocks Mongrel worker threads indefinitely and cascades back to the caller. A looping agent would exhaust the worker pool and take the storefront down with it.
SQL Server slowness propagates directly to callers as hung requests.
No timeouts, retry policy or circuit breaking on external dependency calls.

A slow or failing warehouse/payment dependency propagates straight back to the caller as a hung request. Combined with agent-speed retries this produces connection exhaustion and amplified load on the downstream dependency, with no breaker to shed it.

items.common_finding_summary: Every service in the portfolio lacks schema versioning and a contract-change policy. Breaking changes are shipped without a version bump, deprecation window or consumer notification.
items.root_cause_pattern: Explicit API/schema version in the path or media type; contract tests in CI; a published deprecation policy.
items.remediation: Publish one portfolio API-versioning and deprecation policy and enforce it with contract tests, so an agent's tool definitions do not silently break.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Publish one portfolio API-versioning and deprecation policy and enforce it with contract tests, so an agent's tool definitions do not silently break.
remediation_detail.target_state: Publish one portfolio API-versioning and deprecation policy and enforce it with contract tests, so an agent's tool definitions do not silently break.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: Schema and contract changes are undetectable and unversioned, so any caller binding to this data — including an agent tool definition — breaks silently when the .mdb schema changes.
The documents schema and the page contract can both change with no version signal and no detection, so any agent tool binding would break silently and without warning.
Any column rename or type change in `tickets_ticket` silently breaks the raw SQL in tickets/views.py and any agent tool bound to it, with no versioning or CI detection to catch it.
Any change to the form fields or the applications table is invisible to callers and would silently break agent tool bindings.
Nothing detects or communicates a breaking contract change: an agent tool binding would break silently, and the database schema has no versioned definition in the repository at all.
Consumers reverse-engineer byte offsets from code. Any field addition or width change silently breaks every downstream parser with no version marker or detection gate.

Any change to the query parameters, the HTML output structure, or the rules.dat column layout silently breaks agent tool bindings, and nothing in the build detects it. README.md notes the rules file has 'no source of truth', so the data contract can change outside version control entirely.
The order schema is only discoverable by reading controller code and querying MySQL, and any change to it would break agent tool bindings silently.
Schema and contract are undocumented and unversioned; changes are silent.
A breaking schema edit (removing a field, tightening nullability) would merge undetected and silently break agent tool bindings.
No versioned, documented contract for either the tool interface or the claims schema.
A breaking change to a route or payload can ship with nothing detecting it, and agent tool bindings - which have no version-pinned URL to bind to - would break silently at runtime.
A breaking edit to a schema or an operationId passes CI unchallenged, so agent tool bindings generated from this spec can break silently on deploy.

items.common_finding_summary: Responses carry no temporal metadata — no `as_of`, `last_modified` or freshness indicator — so an agent cannot tell whether it is reasoning over current or stale data. Nightly batch sync makes this acute for legacy-crm-desktop and legacy-payroll-system.
items.root_cause_pattern: A standard `as_of` / `last_modified` field on every agent-facing read response, plus documented staleness bounds per data source.
items.remediation: Add a uniform freshness field to agent-facing responses and document the staleness bound of each backing store, especially where a nightly batch sits between the source and the agent.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Add a uniform freshness field to agent-facing responses and document the staleness bound of each backing store, especially where a nightly batch sits between the source and the agent.
remediation_detail.target_state: Add a uniform freshness field to agent-facing responses and document the staleness bound of each backing store, especially where a nightly batch sits between the source and the agent.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: Timestamps are unnormalized client local time and there is no update timestamp or staleness/consistency signal, so a caller cannot reliably reason about record age or whether data it reads is current.

Timestamps are upload-time only, rendered date-only with no timezone, and no response metadata signals whether the data returned is current. An agent reasoning about document recency cannot establish ordering within a day or detect staleness.
Callers receive no timestamps at all and no freshness or staleness indicator, so an agent cannot reason about how current a ticket record is.
Records carry no timestamps, so an agent cannot determine when an application was created or whether the data it reads is current.
An order carries no record of when it was submitted, so neither an agent nor an operator can reason about ordering, recency, or duplicate timing; and no read path exists that could signal staleness.
An agent cannot determine which pay period a record belongs to, when the underlying data was last updated, or whether the embedded tax constants are current.
An agent can order results by creation time but cannot tell whether a record it reads is current, stale, or cached, and has no last-modified signal for change detection.
No record-provenance timestamps and no freshness signalling.
Agents receive possibly-stale eventually-consistent reads with no indication that they are stale, and have no creation timestamp to reason with.
Timezone-ambiguous timestamps and no freshness signal on retrieved or remembered data.

An agent cannot tell when an order was placed or last modified, nor whether a response reflects the current state - which removes the basis for any time-sensitive decision (for example, whether a refund window has elapsed) and for detecting staleness.
No updated_at field on ledger entities and no machine-readable signal of read consistency, so an agent cannot tell whether a charge it just wrote and immediately read back is current.

items.common_finding_summary: API test coverage of agent-reachable paths is minimal to nonexistent; the mutating paths that most need coverage are the least tested.
items.root_cause_pattern: Integration tests per agent-callable operation, including idempotency, authorization-denial and rollback cases, enforced by a coverage gate.
items.remediation: Require integration test coverage of every agent-callable operation — including negative authorization and retry cases — before that operation is exposed to an agent.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Require integration test coverage of every agent-callable operation — including negative authorization and retry cases — before that operation is exposed to an agent.
remediation_detail.target_state: Require integration test coverage of every agent-callable operation — including negative authorization and retry cases — before that operation is exposed to an agent.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: No test coverage at all on the only data-mutating code path, so behavioural changes (including regressions in SQL construction or error handling) would reach production undetected.
The behaviour of the two entry points is entirely unverified, so no change can be shown not to alter the contract a caller depends on.
Input handling, output format, and error behavior of the endpoints an agent would consume are completely unverified, including the raw SQL paths flagged in DATA-Q4.
No automated coverage of input handling, output values, or error behavior for the operations an agent would call.
Nothing validates input handling, response format, error behaviour, or edge cases on the one operation agents would call, so behavioural regressions would surface only in production.
Payroll calculation logic (gross, FICA, net) has zero regression coverage, so behaviour changes that would mislead an agent — or miscalculate pay — are caught only by manual QA inspection.
Behaviour of the endpoints an agent would consume is unverified. Changes to request handling, response shape, or error semantics would go undetected.
No automated verification of input handling, output shape, or error behaviour.
No automated test exercises the API contract that agents bind to, and no CI would run them if they existed (ENG-Q2).
Agent-facing tool behaviour is largely untested, including every error and edge case.

The agent-facing API has zero automated coverage: no test asserts the auth role checks in src/auth.ts, the 404 path, the error body shape, or the behaviour of the three irreversible operations. The README's claim of a healthy test suite is contradicted by the repository contents.

Error-path and refund behaviour are untested, and the committed suite cannot actually execute because its central fixture is missing, which means the CI pytest step is not providing the assurance it appears to.

items.common_finding_summary: There is no sandbox or staging environment where agent behaviour can be rehearsed. Agents would have to be trialled against production data.
items.root_cause_pattern: A production-like staging environment with synthetic or masked data, and agent-specific smoke suites run there first.
items.remediation: Provide one shared staging environment with masked data as the mandatory first target for any new agent integration.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Provide one shared staging environment with masked data as the mandatory first target for any new agent integration.
remediation_detail.target_state: Provide one shared staging environment with masked data as the mandatory first target for any new agent integration.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: Because the database path is a compile-time constant pointing at production, there is no way to exercise the write path against production-shaped data without touching live customer records.

There is no environment with production-equivalent data shape in which agent behaviour could be rehearsed, so the first execution of any new integration would be against live documents and the live database.
There is no non-production target with production-equivalent data shape, so the first execution of any agent against this system would be against live helpdesk data.
The only test environment is a shared UAT instance with no isolation, no reproducible data shape and no automated provisioning, and the code's default target is production.
There is no environment with production-equivalent data shape where agent behaviour can be exercised safely; the first execution of an agent workflow would hit the live partner order table.

A shared QA region with no committed configuration and no production-shaped synthetic data is not a safe, reproducible place to exercise agent behaviour, and promotion requires hand-editing hardcoded dataset names.

There is no production-shaped environment in which to exercise agent behaviour. Agent testing would either run against a one-row sample dataset that cannot validate real pricing logic, or against production rules.
There is no safe place to exercise agent behaviour: any test of the order flow charges a real card against the live gateway. Agent bugs would first surface in production.
No non-production environment in which to test agent behaviour.
No production-shaped environment in which agent behaviour against the catalog can be exercised before it touches live data.
No production-shaped environment to exercise agent behaviour safely.

There is no environment with production-equivalent data shape in which agent behaviour against the irreversible refund/cancel/delete operations can be exercised safely. The first execution of an agent against these endpoints would be against live data.

items.common_finding_summary: Structured logging and distributed tracing are missing or half-present — X-Ray enabled with no structured logs (modern-catalog-graphql), a documented pino/CloudWatch stack that is not actually installed (modern-orders-service), and plain-text `logging.basicConfig` with no correlation id (modern-claims-agent). No trace context propagates between services.
items.root_cause_pattern: A shared structured-logging library emitting a correlation id, trace-context propagation (`traceparent` / X-Ray) on every hop, and CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled per account.
items.remediation: Mandate one structured-logging format with a propagated correlation id across the portfolio, and enable transaction search so a single agent session can be traced end to end.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Mandate one structured-logging format with a propagated correlation id across the portfolio, and enable transaction search so a single agent session can be traced end to end.
remediation_detail.target_state: Mandate one structured-logging format with a propagated correlation id across the portfolio, and enable transaction search so a single agent session can be traced end to end.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: Failures are unobservable. There is no trace, log line, or correlation identifier with which to reconstruct what happened during any request, agent-initiated or human.

There is no correlation identifier and no application log, so a failed request cannot be reconstructed. An agent-initiated failure would be indistinguishable from any other request in the server logs.
An agent-initiated request cannot be correlated across the request path, and there is no trace ID or request ID to pivot on when a call fails.
A failed agent-initiated submission leaves no correlated trace or log record, so it cannot be reconstructed or attributed.
An agent-initiated submission cannot be traced or correlated. When a call fails or times out, there is no log line, no request id, and no trace to reconstruct what happened inside the service.
An agent-initiated run cannot be correlated end-to-end (API facade to batch job to FTP hop), and there is no structured record of what the run did, making failures effectively undiagnosable.

An agent-initiated failure cannot be reconstructed. There is no per-request identifier linking the agent's call to anything inside the service, no structured fields to query, and no trace context propagation.

An agent-initiated failure — for example a `create` that saved an order but failed the charge — cannot be reconstructed: there is no correlation ID linking the inbound request, the database write, and the gateway call.
Requests cannot be correlated or reconstructed after failure.
X-Ray gives request-level timing but no correlated application log lines, so an agent-initiated failure inside a resolver cannot be reconstructed.
No trace propagation and no structured, correlatable logs across the three hops.

Neither distributed tracing nor correlated structured logging is actually present, so an agent-initiated request that fails cannot be reconstructed: there is no trace linking the API call to the SQL statement and the downstream warehouse/payment call, and no id to correlate log lines for a single request.

items.category: Alerting on Error Rates and Latency
items.common_finding_summary: No service alerts on agent-relevant signals: no error-rate, latency or throughput alarms, and no anomaly detection on call volume.
items.root_cause_pattern: CloudWatch alarms on error rate, p99 latency and invocation volume per agent client, with anomaly detection on agent traffic.
items.remediation: Define a standard agent-traffic alarm set (error rate, latency, volume anomaly) and apply it to every agent-facing service, so a runaway agent is detected in minutes.

remediation_detail.immediate_action: Define a standard agent-traffic alarm set (error rate, latency, volume anomaly) and apply it to every agent-facing service, so a runaway agent is detected in minutes.

items.common_finding_summary: Input validation is absent or partial: free-text parameters interpolated into SQL and shell commands in the legacy services, and no schema enforcement on request bodies in the modern ones.
items.root_cause_pattern: Request-schema validation at the edge (API Gateway models / JSON Schema) plus parameterised queries everywhere.
items.remediation: Enforce request-schema validation at the perimeter for every agent-facing endpoint and eliminate string-interpolated query construction on those paths.

affected_services.resolution_reasoning: Malformed or adversarial input is accepted and executed as SQL. A caller cannot self-correct because rejections are neither structured nor, in most cases, reported at all. This is an exploitable SQL injection path, reachable by anything that can set the Name value.

Both entry points accept arbitrary input shapes with no validation and interpolate them into SQL and into a filesystem path. Malformed or hostile input is neither rejected nor reported; it reaches the database and the filesystem, and failures surface as ColdFusion error pages with no field-level detail.

Unvalidated input is concatenated into SQL — an exploitable SQL injection path — and there are no structured field-level validation errors for an agent to self-correct against. Unescaped output concatenation is an additional stored/reflected XSS path.
Malformed or hostile input is neither rejected nor reported per-field; the only write path is open to SQL injection through the applicant name, and numeric inputs are unbounded.

No validation at the boundary and no structured rejection. Malformed agent payloads either crash into a generic "ERROR:" string or are written through; worse, unvalidated input reaches both an XXE-capable parser and string-built SQL. This is severe evidence recorded at the RISK-QUALITY severity this question carries.
Malformed or out-of-range input (negative/absurd hours, corrupt packed fields, truncated records) is silently computed into a payout rather than rejected with a field-level error.

Malformed inputs are not rejected — they are either silently coerced (qty) or overflow fixed buffers (sku, query string). An agent constructing a long or odd SKU crashes or corrupts the process instead of receiving a field-level rejection, and the unescaped reflection is an XSS sink for any browser-rendered consumer.

Malformed or hostile agent-constructed payloads are neither rejected nor reported. Unparameterised interpolation permits SQL injection; unrestricted mass assignment lets a caller set any Order column, including payment and status fields.
No schema enforcement or field-level rejection, plus SQL injection exposure on read and write.
No boundary validation of model-generated arguments and no structured field-level rejection.

A TypeScript cast is a compile-time assertion with no runtime effect: malformed agent payloads are inserted as NULL/undefined columns or forwarded as an invalid refund amount rather than rejected, and no field-level error is returned that an agent could use to self-correct.

portfolio_level_findings.title: Centralized Identity Plane
portfolio_level_findings.finding: No shared identity provider spans the portfolio. Three services authenticate machine callers independently — modern-payments-api and modern-catalog-graphql each validate OAuth2/JWT against a Cognito user pool supplied as a per-stack `UserPoolId` parameter, and modern-orders-service validates RS256 tokens against its own remote JWKS with audience `orders-service`. No pool, issuer ARN or app-client registry is referenced by more than one repository, and the remaining ten services have no machine-identity mechanism at all (AUTH-Q1 BLOCKER in 10 of 13).
portfolio_level_findings.evidence: modern-payments-api: `infra/template.yaml` UserPoolId parameter + `src/payments/authorizer.py`. modern-catalog-graphql: `infra/template.yaml` CognitoJwt default authorizer, audience `[catalog]`. modern-orders-service: `src/auth.ts` createRemoteJWKSet, audience `orders-service`. modern-claims-agent: MCP gateway `AuthorizerType: NONE`. No shared issuer appears in 2+ repos; no `shared_infra` dependency was declared or inferable.
portfolio_level_findings.recommendation: Designate one identity plane for the portfolio — promote an existing Cognito user pool to shared, or stand up a new one — with one app client per agent and per-agent scopes. Front the ten services lacking machine identity with an API Gateway authorizer against that pool. This single investment is the prerequisite for AUTH-Q2, AUTH-Q3, AUTH-Q6 and AUTH-Q7 remediation.
portfolio_level_findings.affected_services: All 13 services. Directly blocking: the 10 services with AUTH-Q1 BLOCKER. Partially mitigated but unintegrated: modern-payments-api, modern-catalog-graphql, modern-orders-service.
portfolio_level_findings.contextual_annotations: Provides context for cross-cutting BLOCKER AUTH-Q1 — three services already run OAuth2/JWT machine auth, so the portfolio does not start from zero, but because each uses a separate issuer the capability is not shared. **Verify** whether the Cognito pools behind modern-payments-api and modern-catalog-graphql are in fact the same pool in different stacks before planning a new one.

portfolio_level_findings.title: Cross-Service Audit Correlation
portfolio_level_findings.finding: Agent actions cannot be correlated across services. No repository declares an `AWS::CloudTrail::Trail`, no shared audit bucket or log-group naming convention appears in more than one repo, and trace-context propagation is absent: only modern-orders-service mentions `X-Amzn-Trace-Id` at all, modern-catalog-graphql enables X-Ray without emitting a single structured log line, and modern-claims-agent uses plain-text `logging.basicConfig` with no `request_id`, `session_id` or `traceparent`. OBS-Q1 is RISK-QUALITY in 12 of 13 services and AUTH-Q6 is a BLOCKER in all 10 write-enabled services.
portfolio_level_findings.evidence: modern-claims-agent: `ClaimsTranscriptLogs` mutable CloudWatch group, no trail, no Object Lock; `docs/security-review-TODO.md` states an end-to-end session cannot be reconstructed. modern-payments-api: no `AWS::CloudTrail::Trail`, no log retention policy, no S3 Object Lock in `infra/template.yaml`. modern-orders-service: README claims a pino/CloudWatch stack that `package.json` does not contain.
portfolio_level_findings.recommendation: Create one organization CloudTrail trail with log-file validation delivering to an Object-Lock audit bucket, mandate a single structured log schema carrying a propagated correlation id, and enable CloudWatch Transaction Search in the accounts hosting agent-facing services.
portfolio_level_findings.affected_services: All 13 services; most acute for the 10 write-enabled services where AUTH-Q6 is a BLOCKER.
portfolio_level_findings.contextual_annotations: Provides context for cross-cutting BLOCKER AUTH-Q6 — the per-service audit gap and the portfolio correlation gap share one fix (immutable sink plus propagated correlation id). **Verify** that each service's log group is in scope of the new trail and that retention is bounded rather than indefinite.

portfolio_level_findings.title: Portfolio-Level Rate Limiting
portfolio_level_findings.finding: No shared perimeter protects the portfolio from agent traffic storms, and no service has its own rate limiting either — STATE-Q5 is RISK-SAFETY in 11 of 13 services. No WAF WebACL is declared in any repository, no API Gateway usage plan exists (modern-payments-api, modern-catalog-graphql and modern-claims-agent all declare auth but no throttling), modern-orders-service sits behind an ALB with no WAF and no API Gateway, and modern-catalog-graphql additionally imposes no GraphQL depth or complexity limit.
portfolio_level_findings.evidence: modern-catalog-graphql: `infra/template.yaml` declares `Auth` only — no RouteSettings/DefaultRouteSettings throttle, no usage plan, no WAF. modern-payments-api: `infra/template.yaml:36-56` sets StageName/Tracing/Auth/Domain but no MethodSettings throttle; DynamoDB is PAY_PER_REQUEST so there is no capacity ceiling either. modern-claims-agent: gateway and runtime declare no throttle, no reserved concurrency, `NetworkMode: PUBLIC`.
portfolio_level_findings.recommendation: Deploy a shared AWS WAF WebACL with rate-based rules in front of the agent-facing perimeter and per-agent-client API Gateway usage plans, plus reserved concurrency on agent-invoked functions. Because the gap is simultaneously portfolio-level and per-service, the perimeter control should land first as it protects all services at once.
portfolio_level_findings.affected_services: All 13 services; the 11 with STATE-Q5 RISK-SAFETY have no compensating control at any layer.
portfolio_level_findings.contextual_annotations: Provides context for cross-cutting RISK-SAFETY STATE-Q5. **Verify** that a perimeter rate limit is actually on the agent call path for modern-orders-service, which is ALB-fronted rather than API Gateway-fronted.

portfolio_level_findings.title: Transitive Dependency Safety
portfolio_level_findings.finding: This question could not be evaluated as specified. No `dependency_overrides` were supplied in the portfolio configuration, and no inter-service dependency could be inferred from the per-repo reports: an exhaustive scan of all 13 ARA report JSONs found zero mentions of any other portfolio service name in any finding, evaluation, evidence or context field. Without a dependency graph there are no sync chains to trace, so no transitive BLOCKER can be asserted. Note that the latent exposure is high — 8 of 13 services are Not Agent-Integrable, so any undeclared sync dependency on one of them would block an otherwise-ready caller.
portfolio_level_findings.evidence: Scan of all 13 `*-ara-report.json` files for the other 12 repo names (exact and suffix match): 0 hits. No `shared_db`, `shared_infra` or client-stub references to sibling services appear in any report.
portfolio_level_findings.recommendation: Supply `dependency_overrides` in the portfolio configuration (source, target, type, description) and re-run the portfolio analysis. Until then, treat the readiness profile of each service as valid only for calls that terminate in that service.
portfolio_level_findings.affected_services: Unknown — no dependency edges are known. Re-evaluate once dependency data is supplied.
portfolio_level_findings.contextual_annotations: None. No individual finding is contextualised by this result.

portfolio_level_findings.title: Agent Identity Governance
portfolio_level_findings.finding: There is no portfolio-wide agent identity registry and no centralized revocation path. AUTH-Q7 is RISK-SAFETY in 11 of 13 services: modern-claims-agent has one shared execution role assumed by both runtime and tool Lambda, so disabling it takes down the attended adjuster path as well; modern-orders-service validates tokens statelessly against a remote JWKS with no denylist, `jti` check or introspection; modern-payments-api could in principle disable a Cognito app client but declares no app-client resources and documents no revocation procedure. No central inventory of agent identities exists in any repository.
portfolio_level_findings.evidence: modern-claims-agent: `claims-agent-execution` role shared by runtime and tool Lambda; gateway has no authorizer, so there are no per-agent credentials at all. modern-orders-service: `src/auth.ts` createRemoteJWKSet with no denylist and no per-client enable/disable flag. modern-payments-api: `infra/template.yaml` carries only a UserPoolId parameter; `RUNBOOK.md` documents no revocation step.
portfolio_level_findings.recommendation: Maintain one agent identity registry at the shared identity plane (one app client per agent, tagged with owner and scope), add a denylist or introspection check on token validation paths, and publish a single portfolio kill-switch runbook that revokes an agent everywhere in one action.
portfolio_level_findings.affected_services: All 13 services; the 11 with AUTH-Q7 RISK-SAFETY have no per-agent revocation path today.
portfolio_level_findings.contextual_annotations: Provides context for cross-cutting RISK-SAFETY AUTH-Q7 and depends on PORT-ARA-Q1 — per-agent revocation is only possible once per-agent identities exist. **Verify** that revoking an app client actually terminates in-flight sessions rather than only blocking new token issuance.
